title: Writing to clarify your thinking
text: Writing helps you find out what you think, as well as report what you already know. For further reading, see the section Writing to clarify your thinking in the UCD-SERG lab manual.

title: Writing to clarify your thinking
text:
1 Write the question down first
When a question or idea comes up, write it down right away, before you search for an answer or ask anyone. Writing it down does three things:

It organizes your thoughts and shows you what you need to know.
It forces you to state the problem precisely.
It often leads you to the answer.

Leslie Lamport, a computer scientist who won the Turing Award, argues that thinking without writing is only the feeling of thinking (Lamport 2019). If you cannot write an idea down clearly, you probably do not understand it yet.

title: Writing for teaching
text:
NoteAI-Assisted Authorship



This chapter was written with the assistance of GitHub Copilot, which expanded on outlined ideas and draft notes provided by the author. The content represents the author’s perspective and has been reviewed for accuracy, but the detailed prose was generated through AI assistance.
Lecture notes, slides, and problem sets teach rather than report. The general rules for scientific writing in the other chapters still apply. This chapter adds the rules that apply to teaching materials in particular.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 1 Build the lecture from exercises and solutions
text:
1 Build the lecture from exercises and solutions
Active learning, in which students work through tasks themselves during class, improves exam performance over lecture alone (Freeman et al. 2014). The exercise-first structure is this guide’s own convention for putting that result into practice. Pose each task as an exercise, give students time to try it, and then show the solution.

Pose every data manipulation or analysis as an exercise, and show the code in the solution. Do not show the code first and explain it afterwards.
Pose every calculation, derivation, or proof as an exercise, and put the worked steps in the solution.
Ask the question that a definition or theorem answers before stating it. The solution answers informally, in plain words, and the formal #def- or #thm- div follows the solution div.
Give each bottom-level prompt its own #exr- div and its own #sol- div, in order, rather than one exercise with parts (a) through (e). Any exercise with several parts is split, however the parts are marked: letters, numbers or bullets. Put the shared setup in the first exercise, and begin each later exercise by citing it, as in “Make the assumptions of the first exercise.” Later exercises can use earlier results through cross-references.
On slides, put a slide break between an exercise and its solution, so the prompt is on screen alone while students work.
Give each solution the slug of its exercise, with sol- in place of exr-.
Put a hint in a callout titled “Hint” inside the exercise div, not in italic text.








Example 1 (Asking before defining)  

❌ Generalization is the ability of a model to perform well on new data.


✅
::: {#exr-generalization}
What does it mean for a model to generalize?
:::

::: {#sol-generalization}
A model generalizes when it predicts well on data it was not fit to.
:::

::: {#def-generalization}
(the formal definition)
:::

The revised version lets students attempt the idea before they see the formal definition.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 2 Build every unit from smaller atomic units
text:
2 Build every unit from smaller atomic units
Make every unit of analysis as concise and minimal as possible. The units are mathematical expressions and divs of every kind: definitions, theorems, lemmas, corollaries, examples, remarks and proofs. When a unit grows complicated, do not write the complexity into it. Abstract the complexity out into smaller, atomic definitions, results and expressions, each with its own name and identifier, and glue the pieces together with hyperlinks.
This is the compositional approach of modular programming: a program is built from small, single-purpose modules that call one another, and a maintainer changes one module without reading the rest. The notes work the same way. A theorem links to the definitions it uses, a proof links to the lemmas it uses, and an expression is written with the named pieces it is built from.

A display holds one idea. Name each meaningful sub-expression, give it a macro, and build the display from the names (see Making expressions concise).
A div holds one term or one result. Move a second term, a side property or a long argument into its own div, and link to it from the place that needs it (see Give each defined term its own div).
A proof states the lemmas it needs and links to them, instead of deriving them in the middle of the argument.
A link replaces a repeated explanation. If a piece is already written, link to it instead of writing it a second time.

When a unit still looks long, ask what could be named and moved out.







Example 2 (Splitting one long definition)  

❌ One div defines the ridge estimator, defines its penalty, and proves that it shrinks the coefficients.
✅ Three divs: a definition of the penalty, a definition of the ridge estimator that links to the penalty, and a theorem on shrinkage that links to both.

The ✅ version lets a later chapter link to the penalty alone, and each piece fits on a slide.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 3 Give each defined term its own div
text:
3 Give each defined term its own div
Defining terms clearly covers what a good definition contains. For teaching materials, four further rules keep definitions findable.

Replace a bolded keyword in running prose with a #def- div. A bolded keyword usually marks an inline definition.
Define one term per #def- div. A term defined inside another term’s div, or two terms joined in one title (“Regression and classification”), has no identifier of its own, so nothing can link to it.
Never nest one theorem-type div inside another. The rule covers #def-, #thm-, #lem-, #cor-, #prp-, #cnj-, #exm-, #rem-, #exr-, and #sol-. A special case, such as a linear evaluation function, gets its own div after the general case, and the two link to each other.
Keep only the definition in a #def- div. Put the properties of the defined object, such as the symmetry and idempotence of a matrix, in a separate #thm-, #lem- or #prp- div after it, with a proof where one is known. Each abstract div then gets its own example, as the rule below requires.

Every alternative name for the same concept stays in the div of the term it names and is treated like the primary name: it appears in the div title and is bold where it first appears in the definition. Name synonyms and near-synonyms where the term is defined, and say which one the notes use. A student who meets one name here and another in a textbook cannot tell whether the difference matters. For a near-synonym, name the seam: critical points include the stationary points and also the points where the derivative does not exist.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 4 State the notation and its alternatives
text:
4 State the notation and its alternatives
When a symbol or convention has more than one common form, state the one the notes use and name the others a reader will meet elsewhere. Put the alternatives in the definition div or in a callout beside it. For example, some sources include 0 in the natural numbers and others exclude it, so write \(\mathbb{N}_0\) or \(\mathbb{N}^+\) to make the choice explicit.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 5 Lead with the simplest correct form of a definition
text:
5 Lead with the simplest correct form of a definition
Define a quantity in the form that needs the fewest symbols, and state the textbook form as a theorem that follows. For example, define variance as the mean squared deviation \(\operatorname{E}\left[\operatorname{devn}(X)^2\right]\), where \(\operatorname{devn}(X) = X - \operatorname{E}[X]\), and then prove that it equals \(\operatorname{E}[X^2] - (\operatorname{E}[X])^2\).
Parsimony outranks convention when choosing a primary definition. The conventional form still appears in the notes, as a named result.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 6 Reuse one written version of each result
text:
6 Reuse one written version of each result
When several courses or repositories have already written the same definition, theorem, or exercise, compare the versions on notation, decomposition, parsimony, and clarity. Use the best one, or merge them, and make it the single copy. Other places include or link to that copy instead of keeping a second wording that can drift.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 7 Use real data and compute every number
text:
7 Use real data and compute every number

Where an example needs data, use a real dataset instead of invented round numbers. Name its original source, link to where it is published, and cite it.
Show a dataset before analyzing it, with a printed look at its first rows and its structure.
Show the data where it is first mentioned. Put a table of a few rows, or a plot of the variables, directly after the sentence that names the dataset, before any discussion of its features, the methods to apply to it, or the questions it raises. A reader who has seen the data can picture what the next slides describe, while a reader who has not must hold an abstract description in mind until the data appears. If the data are too large to show, show a sample or a summary figure. Link later mentions of the dataset back to this first display.
Never type or paste output. The page shows what the code printed when the page was rendered, and each number in the prose comes from inline code. A number typed into prose goes stale when the data or the code changes.








Example 3 (Showing the data at first mention)  

❌ Slides 3 to 9 discuss the spam data’s 57 predictors, its class imbalance and the loss we will minimize. Slide 10 shows a table of the first rows.
✅ Slide 3 introduces the spam data and shows a table of its first rows and a plot of one predictor by class. Slides 4 to 10 discuss the predictors, the class imbalance and the loss, and refer back to that table and plot.

The ✅ version lets every later slide refer to something the reader has already seen.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 8 Store structured data in structured formats
text:
8 Store structured data in structured formats
This rule applies to all teaching materials, in every course and every teaching repository.

Keep a list or table of like items, such as courses, readings, channels or glossary terms, in a CSV, YAML or JSON file with one record per item. The page reads the file and builds the table or list with a short function, instead of holding a hand-written Markdown table.
A data file can be counted, filtered, sorted and reused by another page, and a new row is a one-line change that a reviewer reads as data.
List the file under the page’s resources: when the site publishes it.
Convert an existing hand-written table in its own pull request, and render the page before and after to confirm that the output text is identical.
A short list that no other page reads can stay as prose.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 9 Show each idea applied and in a figure
text:
9 Show each idea applied and in a figure

Give every definition, method and result at least one applied example that computes it on real data, so the reader sees what the idea does before or beside the algebra.
Follow every abstract div directly with a concrete #exm- div. The rule covers each #def-, #thm-, #lem-, #cor- and similar div. The example of a related result does not exempt a definition: a theorem that uses a definition gets its own example, and so does the definition. The ai-config rule links here.
Give every topic at least one figure that shows the idea, such as the data with a fitted curve, a distribution, or a diagram of the procedure. A page of definitions with no figure and no data is incomplete.
Prerequisite notes follow the same rule as course lectures. A prerequisite page that is only definitions and algebra needs an applied example and a figure.
Place each figure directly after the sentence that first refers to it. Do not refer to a figure, table, or result that appears later in the document, because the reader meets the reference before the thing it points to. This rule is for teaching materials, which are reading copies. A journal submission may collect its figures at the end, as Figures and tables describes.
Make each figure follow the accessibility rules below.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 10 Follow every example with an exercise and solution
text:
10 Follow every example with an exercise and solution
Reading a worked example is passive. A reader who has just seen one method applied learns more by applying it to a new case than by reading a second example. So each example gets a practice exercise, with its solution, right after it.

After every #exm- div, add an #exr- div that asks the reader to do the same thing for a different case, followed by its #sol- div. The exercise changes the data, the function or the question, so the solution is not a copy of the example.
The full sequence for a new idea is therefore: the exercise that poses the question and its solution, the definition or theorem, an example, and a practice exercise with its solution.
More generally, give readers an opportunity to think at every stage: a question they can answer before the next paragraph, a calculation to try, a prediction to make before the code runs.
A counterexample (see Defining terms clearly) can stand in for the practice exercise when the exercise would be “decide whether this case fits the definition”.
Give the practice exercise its own slug and follow the numbering and slide-break rules above.








Example 4 (An example followed by a practice exercise)  

✅
::: {#exm-sample-mean}
(the sample mean of one variable in a real dataset, computed by a code chunk)
:::

::: {#exr-sample-mean-new-variable}
Compute the sample mean of a different variable in the same dataset.
:::

::: {#sol-sample-mean-new-variable}
(the code chunk and its output)
:::

The example shows the method once. The exercise asks the reader to repeat it on a new variable before moving on, and the solution’s numbers still come from running code (see Use real data and compute every number).

title: Writing for teaching
section: 11 Write labs for both languages and any computer
text:
11 Write labs for both languages and any computer
These rules apply to all teaching materials, in every course and every teaching repository, not only to one course.

Give labs and code exercises in both R and Python, side by side.
Put each step’s Python and R pair in its own tabset with group="language". Start a new tabset whenever prose or a new step sits between code chunks, so the reader sees one step’s code in one language at a time. The shared group makes one choice of language apply to every tabset on the page, as long as the tab headings use identical text in every tabset, such as always “R” and “Python”.
Write the R code with tidymodels, or show tidymodels and base R side by side. Do not give base R alone. ISLR-tidymodels-labs shows the style.
When a lab follows a textbook’s lab, use the book’s exercises, data and fitting functions, in the book’s order. For the ISL labs, fit Python models with statsmodels’ sm.OLS, as ISLP_labs does. If an exercise departs from the book, say why in the lab.
Never throw away an exercise you replace. Either keep both exercises, or keep the replaced one as an outtake: leave its file in place and stop including it.
Tell students where to get the data.
Point students only to places they can open. Students read a course’s published site, not its repository, which is often private. So never send them to a file in the repository, to a github.com link into a private repository, or to “the copy in this repository”. Link a data file from the published site, from a public repository or package, or from the data’s original public source.
Do not assume that students own a laptop. Assume only that they can use some computer, so setup steps must work on a shared or hosted machine.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 12 Present R results with modern packages
text:
12 Present R results with modern packages
This rule applies to all R code in teaching materials, in every course and every teaching repository.

Even when you fit a model with a base R function such as lm() or glm(), show its results with modern packages, not with base R output.
Show coefficient tables with parameters (parameters() |> print_md()) or gtsummary (tbl_regression()), not with summary() or coef(summary()) printouts.
Draw figures with ggplot2, not with base graphics such as plot(), lines() and abline().
Draw model plots with packages built on ggplot2: sjPlot or ggeffects for predictions, and performance’s check_model() for diagnostic plots.
Show model fit statistics with performance’s model_performance() or broom’s glance().
Ezra’s rme notes show the style.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 13 Manipulate data with dplyr, not base R
text:
13 Manipulate data with dplyr, not base R
This rule applies to all R code in teaching materials, in every course and every teaching repository.

Select columns with dplyr’s select(), not with df[, c("a", "b")] or df[c("a", "b")].
Filter rows with filter(), not with df[df$x > 0, ] or subset().
Add or change columns with mutate(), not with df$new <- ....
Drop rows with missing values with tidyr’s drop_na(), not with df[complete.cases(df), ].
Stack data frames with bind_rows(), not with rbind().
Build data frames with tibble’s tibble(), not with data.frame().
Chain steps with the native pipe |>.
Do not nest function calls. Write tibble(x, y) |> pander(), not pander(tibble(x, y)), and sizes |> lapply(f) |> bind_rows(), not bind_rows(lapply(sizes, f)). Give a call that would sit inside an argument, such as data = filter(df, train) in a model call, a name on its own line first.
Reading one value out of a data frame for inline code is fine, as is indexing a matrix or a vector. The rule is about selecting, filtering and building data frames.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 14 Include code from files instead of copying it
text:
14 Include code from files instead of copying it
This rule applies to code that appears in more than one place in teaching materials.

When the same code appears in several pages, or in a page and a script, keep one source file and include it where it is shown. A copy in each place drifts when one copy is fixed and the others are not (see Reuse one written version of each result).
Code that the page runs should be an executed chunk, as above. For code that is displayed but not executed on the page, such as a standalone script or a configuration file, Quarto’s include-code-files extension fills a code block from a file. Add filters: [include-code-files] to the front matter, then write a code block with an include attribute, such as ```{.python include="script.py"}.
The extension also takes start-line and end-line, to show part of a file. Prefer a range that names the lines you want over a copy of those lines.
The extension is a new dependency of the site: install it with quarto add quarto-ext/include-code-files, and commit the _extensions directory it creates.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 15 Comment every code chunk to say what and why
text:
15 Comment every code chunk to say what and why
This rule applies to all reader-facing code in teaching materials, in every course and every teaching repository, in every language.

Put comments in each code chunk that explain both what the code is doing and why it does it.
Leave out a comment that would give away the solution in an exercise prompt. Add the comments to the solution’s code instead.
A comment that only restates the code, such as # add 1 to x above x <- x + 1, gives the what without the why. Say what the step accomplishes and why the analysis needs it, for example # center age so the intercept is the mean outcome at the average age.
Comment each step that a student could not reconstruct from its name, such as a transformation, a modeling choice, a tuning value or a random seed.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 16 Set code-fold by what the code does and whether the prose mentions it
text:
16 Set code-fold by what the code does and whether the prose mentions it
This rule applies to every executed code chunk in teaching materials, in every course and every teaching repository.
Set #| code-fold: on each chunk by two questions: does the prose mention the code, and does the code produce output outside the chunk, such as a figure, a table, or variables that inline expressions use?

#| code-fold: show when the prose mentions the code and the code produces output outside the chunk: a figure, a table, or variables that inline expressions use. The code starts open, and a reader who wants to focus on the output can hide it.
#| code-fold: true when the prose does not mention the code. This holds whether the code produces output outside the chunk or no output at all. The code starts hidden, and a reader who wants it can open it.
#| code-fold: false when the prose mentions the code and the code produces no output, or only output that the chunk renders inside itself. The code and its output stay together, with no toggle.

For example, a chunk that fits a model the text walks through and prints its coefficients is false, a chunk that draws a figure the text discusses is show, and a chunk that loads a package or builds an object that later chunks use is true.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 17 Introduce every function in a programming primer
text:
17 Introduce every function in a programming primer
This rule applies to all teaching materials that run code, in every course and every teaching repository.

Give the course a programming primer that introduces each package function the course’s chapters call. A student meets the function there first, in a short note, a worked example and an exercise, and then sees it used in the chapters.
Keep the primer complete by computing the list of functions, not by remembering it. Scan the code chunks of the chapters for the functions they call, and compare the list with the functions the primer mentions. Run the scan when a chapter adds a function, and again before a term starts.
Add the missing functions in separate pull requests, one per package. A pull request that adds a function to a chapter adds it to the primer too, or links the primer entry that already introduces it.
Functions that a chapter defines for itself are not package functions. A chapter introduces those where it defines them.

title: Writing for teaching
text:
18 Make figures accessible

Wrap each figure, including an interactive one, in a #fig- div with a caption.
Give every plot alt text. For Observable Plot, set ariaLabel.
Show the code that makes each figure, and let readers fold it away. Code folding does nothing for a cell that does not echo its code, so do not set echo: false on a cell you want students to read.
Do not cross-reference an interactive figure from prose, because the PDF format renders no figure for it, so the reference has no target there (observed when rendering lecture notes to PDF).

title: Writing for teaching
text:
19 Structure slides for the reader

Check the rendered slides, not only the web page. Slides need the same boxes and colors on theorem-type and callout divs that the web page has, so a reader can see where a definition ends and the commentary begins.
Put a list of three or more phrases in a bullet list, as Put lists in bullet points describes.
Put each named example in an #exm- div.
Put on a slide only what you want the audience to look at. Put an example in an #exm- div and short commentary in a #rem- div, because a ::: notes div is plain text without a box on the web page.
Put a long paragraph of commentary in a remark that is also speaker notes: ::: {#rem-name .remark .notes}. Reveal.js shows it only in speaker view, so the audience does not have to read it, and the web page shows it as a boxed remark. Readers who did not attend the lecture use the web page, so nothing is lost, and nothing is said twice. Give a long paragraph a separate short #rem- div only when the slide needs a takeaway to look at.
Add structure only where content has a shape. Do not put a heading over a single item, or over the same topic as the heading just before it.
Keep body text off section and title slides. Reveal.js centers those slides vertically and does not scroll them, so long text is clipped at the top and bottom of the screen (observed in lecture slides rendered with Quarto). Put a slide break after the heading and move the text onto content slides.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 20 Talk about the ideas, not the notes
text:
20 Talk about the ideas, not the notes
When a term is defined on another page or in another site, state the idea in the sentence and link the term. Do not write about where the definition lives.

Write “the bias of an estimator”, linked to its definition, not “the statistics notes define the bias of an estimator”.
Do not write “see the probability notes” or “as in our notes”. The link already says where the term lives.
Name a remark by the idea it holds, such as “Bias of a prediction”, not “Bias of a prediction in the statistics notes”.

Students read concepts, not the structure of the site. A sentence about which notes define a term adds no content, and it goes stale when the definition moves.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 21 Credit other courses without summarizing them
text:
21 Credit other courses without summarizing them

Write your own version of another course’s material, and credit the source in a collapsed .callout-note titled “Source”, not in running prose. Adapting another course’s material gives the details, including when a ::: notes div is a safe alternative.
Quote the primary source directly, and check the wording and page against the original. Quote the original explains why.
Title a section by its topic, not by its author or course. Put the content first explains why.
Where the book is the subject rather than its authors, name the book by its title, because a bare citation key renders as the author list.

title: Writing for teaching
section: 22 Rules that apply to all writing

title: Writing for code review and software
text:
Software projects depend on short documents:
Readers of these documents often arrive without context on the change, so the rules in the other chapters apply to them too. This chapter lists the general rules that matter most here and adds a few that belong to software.

title: Writing for code review and software
text:
1 Apply the general rules

Write in the active voice and name the actor before the action.
Limit complex sentence structures: write one main idea per sentence and avoid piling several subordinate clauses into one.
Cut filler and prefer plain words (Word choice).
Scan for clichés before you post non-trivial prose. Skip the scan for code, terse status lines, and short replies, which are too short to contain a cluster of tells.
Put lists in bullet points.

title: Writing for code review and software
text:
2 Say what changed and why

Open a pull request description with the behavior a reader would see before and after the change.
Explain the reason for the change in the commit message, not only the content of the diff.
State what you checked and what you did not.
Link the issue, the data, or the document that motivates the change.


❌ Update plotting code.
✅ Label the y-axis in original units, so the figure no longer shows log-odds.

title: Writing for code review and software
text:
3 Comment code sparingly

Write a comment that says why the code does what it does, and let the code say what it does.
Keep each comment as short as it can be while still giving the reason.
Update or delete a comment when the code changes.

title: Writing for code review and software
section: 4 Check CRAN before you name an R package

title: Writing for code review and software
section: 5 Write release notes for the user
text:
5 Write release notes for the user

Describe each change by its effect on the user, not by the file that changed.
Put breaking changes first, because the user must act on them.

title: Paper organization
text: Effective organization helps readers navigate your scientific paper and understand your findings. The structure of your paper should guide readers logically from your research question through your methods to your results and conclusions.

title: Paper organization
text:
1 Write to clarify your thinking
Write down a question or an idea as soon as you have it, before you search for an answer. Writing it down helps you in these ways:

You see what you need to know.
You state the problem more precisely.
You often answer the question yourself while writing it.

The computer scientist Leslie Lamport argues that a person who thinks without writing only thinks that they are thinking (Lamport 2019).

title: Paper organization
text:
2 Standard paper structure
Most scientific papers follow the IMRaD structure:

Introduction: Present the research question and background
Methods: Describe how the study was conducted
Results: Present the findings
Discussion: Interpret the findings and their implications

Some papers combine Results and Discussion into a single section.

title: Paper organization
text:
3 Organizing the Results section
The Results section presents your findings clearly and logically. How you organize this section depends on your research design and the complexity of your analyses.

3.1 Single outcome studies
When analyzing a single primary outcome, organize results by:

Descriptive statistics first
Main analysis results
Sensitivity analyses or subgroup analyses



3.2 Multiple outcomes analyzed separately
When analyzing multiple outcomes separately, group your results section by outcome rather than by analysis type. This organization improves clarity and readability by keeping all information about each outcome together.

Why group by outcome
Grouping by outcome helps readers:

Follow the story of each outcome from descriptive statistics through final results
Compare findings across outcomes more easily
Understand the complete picture for each outcome before moving to the next
Navigate directly to outcomes of interest



How to organize by outcome
For each outcome, present:

Descriptive statistics
Main analysis results
Sensitivity analyses
Subgroup analyses (if applicable)

Structure:
Results
├── Outcome 1: Mortality
│   ├── Descriptive statistics
│   ├── Main analysis
│   ├── Sensitivity analyses
│   └── Subgroup analyses
├── Outcome 2: Hospital readmission
│   ├── Descriptive statistics
│   ├── Main analysis
│   ├── Sensitivity analyses
│   └── Subgroup analyses
└── Outcome 3: Quality of life
    ├── Descriptive statistics
    ├── Main analysis
    ├── Sensitivity analyses
    └── Subgroup analyses


What to avoid
Don’t group by analysis type when outcomes are analyzed separately:
Results (POOR ORGANIZATION)
├── Descriptive statistics
│   ├── Mortality
│   ├── Hospital readmission
│   └── Quality of life
├── Main analyses
│   ├── Mortality
│   ├── Hospital readmission
│   └── Quality of life
└── Sensitivity analyses
    ├── Mortality
    ├── Hospital readmission
    └── Quality of life
This forces readers to jump back and forth between sections to understand the complete story for any single outcome.


Exception: Shared descriptive statistics
If your descriptive statistics apply to all outcomes (for example, baseline characteristics in a clinical trial), present them once at the beginning before discussing individual outcomes.

title: Paper organization
text:
4 Figures and tables
In a reading copy (a website, a preprint, or a draft circulated to coauthors), place figures and tables near the relevant text that describes them. A journal submission often needs a different layout (Section 4.3). Either way, number figures and tables sequentially and reference them in the text before they appear.
Each figure and table should have a clear, informative caption that allows readers to understand it without reading the main text.

4.1 Label variables in plain words
A figure or table is read by people, not by the code that made it. Replace every variable name from the data with a label a reader understands:

turn underscores and other code punctuation into spaces;
use ordinary capitalization;
spell out abbreviations and acronyms where space allows;
give the unit of every measured quantity, in parentheses;
relabel category levels the same way, including legend entries.

Use the same label for a variable in every figure, table and paragraph, so a reader can match them up.







Example 1 (Relabeling axes and a legend)  

❌ x-axis age_yrs, y-axis sbp, legend trt_grp: ctrl, tx
✅ x-axis “Age (years)”, y-axis “Systolic blood pressure (mm Hg)”, legend “Treatment group”: “Control”, “Treatment”

In R with ggplot2, set the axis and legend titles with labs(), and recode the category levels before plotting, for example with forcats::fct_recode().






4.2 Captions are captions, not headings
Give every figure and table a numbered caption, including those in the supplementary material. A table without a caption is incomplete, even when its contents are correct.
Attach each caption to its figure or table with your writing tool’s caption feature (in Quarto, the last line of a #fig- or #tbl- div), not as a section heading.
Poor caption: a section heading that reads “Supplementary Figure S43: Distribution of follow-up time”, placed above the figure
Better caption: “Distribution of follow-up time”, written as a caption attached to the figure, with its label and number generated by your writing tool rather than typed by hand (a supplementary “S” prefix may need extra setup in the tool)
A heading posing as a caption usually appears in the table of contents, takes on heading styling, and is not attached to its figure. Its number is typed by hand, so it falls out of step with the real numbering when figures are added, removed, or reordered.


4.3 Manuscript layout for journal submission
Many journals ask for figures and tables to follow the main text of a submitted manuscript rather than appear inline. Unless the journal’s instructions say otherwise, lay out a submission manuscript as follows:

Put all main-text figures and tables at the end of the main manuscript, after the main text and the references, and before the supplementary material. The main text still cites each one by number.
Insert a page break before the supplementary material header, so the supplement starts on a new page.
Keep each caption with its figure or table. Insert a page break before the first figure or table and between consecutive ones, so that each one starts on a page where it fits with its caption. Do not let a caption fall on a different page from its figure or table, or split across a page break, unless it cannot be avoided, as when a figure or table and its caption together are taller than a full page.

In Quarto, the {{< pagebreak >}} shortcode inserts a page break in PDF and Word output, and a ::: {#refs} div places the references where you put the div instead of at the end of the document. Write the figures and tables after that div.


4.4 Check the rendered layout
Captions, page breaks, and figure placement are properties of the rendered document’s layout. Problems with them are easy to miss when reading the source, and a check of the text and numbers alone will not catch them. Before calling a rendered manuscript reviewed, page through the PDF or Word output and check its layout, not only its text and numbers:

Does every figure and table have a numbered caption?
Does each caption sit on the same page as its figure or table?
For a journal submission, do the main-text figures and tables come after the references and before the supplement, and does the supplementary material start on a new page?

title: Paper organization
text:
5 Subsection headings
Use descriptive subsection headings to guide readers through your results. Headings should clearly indicate the content of each section.
Poor heading: “Analysis 1”
Better heading: “Association between treatment and mortality”
Best heading: “Treatment reduced mortality by 30%” (when appropriate and not overstating findings)

title: Paper organization
text:
6 Avoid forward references
A forward reference points the reader to content they have not reached yet. Common forms are:

“as discussed below”
“see the next section”
“we will return to this later”
a technical term or result used before the definition or theorem that introduces it

The reader must hold an unresolved pointer while reading the sentence that depends on it.
Fix a forward reference by moving the content ahead of the pointer, so that each definition or result precedes the sentences that use it. Then change “below” to “above”, or delete the directional word. Do not fix a forward reference by removing the hyperlink to the later definition or theorem while leaving the term in the sentence: the sentence still uses a concept the reader has not met, and the reader also loses the link to its definition.
If moving the content would break the order of the argument, keep the pointer, and make it a working link. Say what the link points to and where it is, as in “Table 2 (later in this section)”, with “Table 2” linked to the table. Do not delete the link and leave only the name. The reader then loses both the warning and the jump.







Example 2 (Removing a forward reference)  

❌ The adjusted estimates, discussed in the next section, differ from the crude estimates. The adjustment, described below, uses age and sex.
✅ The adjustment uses age and sex. The adjusted estimates differ from the crude estimates.

In the ❌ version, both pointers send the reader to content that comes later, so the reader sees “adjusted” before the paper says what was adjusted. In the ✅ version, the sentence that defines the adjustment comes first, so neither pointer is needed.




Two cases are not forward references to fix:

An overview near the start that previews the structure, such as “Section 2 describes the data, and Section 3 gives the results”. The reader is not meant to resolve the preview immediately.
A sentence that names a figure or table placed beside it, such as “Table 2 shows the estimates”. The reader meets the table at once.

A word such as “below” in an ordinary comparison, as in “values below the detection limit”, is not a pointer at all.
When you insert or move a section, check the references that name a position, such as “the two sections above” or “the previous section”. Name the target instead, as in “the sections on mortality and morbidity”, so that a later insertion does not make the position wrong.

title: Paper organization
section: 7 Links to videos and other media
text:
7 Links to videos and other media
Put each link to a video, podcast, demo or other external material in a short note right after the text the material supports. Do not collect the links in a list at the end of the document. If the material covers several sections, put the note after the first section the material supports. If the text the note supports is a question followed by its answer, put the note after the answer, not between them.
A reader who has just finished a section is ready to use material about it. The same reader at the end of the document must guess which link goes with which section, and may never reach the list.
For each link:

Write one line, such as “Video: Weinberger derives the descent direction (from 3:09).”
Name the speaker and say what the material shows, in simple, literal words.
Link the exact start time when the material covers more than the topic.
Cite the source.

Link public sites freely. Anyone can open them, so a link costs the reader nothing. Do not link private repositories, such as ones that hold graded homework or exams.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
text:
NoteAI-Assisted Authorship



This chapter was written with the assistance of GitHub Copilot, which expanded on outlined ideas and draft notes provided by the author. The content represents the author’s perspective and has been reviewed for accuracy, but the detailed prose was generated through AI assistance.
A mathematical paper is made of sentences, and the formulas are part of the sentences. This chapter collects rules for fitting formulas into prose. It draws on the lecture notes of a Stanford course on mathematical writing (Knuth et al. 1987). This chapter selects the rules that bear most on formulas. Several of the course’s other rules appear in other chapters, and Table 1 points to them. The notes also cover spelling, punctuation and refereeing, which this book does not.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
text:
1 Keep formulas inside sentences
Readers meet a formula as part of a sentence, so the words around it decide whether the formula can be read.

1.1 Separate formulas with words
Put words between two formulas. Without them, the reader cannot tell where one formula ends and the next begins.







Example 1 (Separating two formulas)  

❌ Define \(f_k\), \(k \ge 2\).
✅ Define \(f_k\), where \(k \ge 2\).

In the ❌ version the comma between the two formulas reads as part of the first one. The ✅ version names the relation between them.






1.2 Do not start a sentence with a symbol
A sentence that starts with a symbol is hard to see as a new sentence, because the formula runs on from the period before it. Start with a word, such as the name of the object.







Example 2 (Starting a sentence with a word)  

❌ \(t^2 - 5\) has two real roots.
✅ The polynomial \(t^2 - 5\) has two real roots.







1.3 Write logical symbols as words
In prose, write “implies”, “for every” and “there exists”, not \(\Rightarrow\), \(\forall\) and \(\exists\). The same goes for the symbols for “therefore” and “such that”. Keep the symbols in a work on logic.


1.4 Test the sentence with the formulas removed
Many readers skim past the formulas on a first reading. Replace each formula by a placeholder such as “blah”. If the sentence no longer reads smoothly, rewrite it.


1.5 Tie formulas together with commentary
A list of formulas with no words between them is the style of a homework paper. Say what each step does and why the next one follows. A sentence such as “Because the set \(S\) has an element, we can pick one and call it \(s\)” tells the reader where the argument is going, and the bare formula does not.


1.6 Make the prose say what the formula says
The sentence that introduces or interprets a formula must describe that formula. Check every term in the sentence against the formula, symbol by symbol. The words and the symbols must name the same quantity, the same data, and the same kind of average. When you change one, change the other in the same edit.







Example 3 (A sentence that names the wrong average) Suppose the formula is \(\E{\paren{\newoutvar - \predvalf{\predvar}}^2}\), a population mean at one covariate value \(\predvar\). The sentence “the average squared error over the training set” does not describe it. It names a sample average over many observations. Write “the expected squared prediction error at \(\predvar\)” instead.




Before you submit, reread each formula next to the sentence that describes it. Do the same after every edit to either one. Related rules cover using one notation for one thing and defining every variable when you introduce it.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
section: 2 Introduce a theorem with a sentence
text:
2 Introduce a theorem with a sentence
The line before a theorem, lemma or algorithm should be a complete sentence, or end with a colon. Do not let a heading such as “Theorem” finish a sentence that began above it.







Example 4 (Introducing a theorem)  

❌ This gives the following Theorem. \(G(x)\) is increasing.
✅ Next we prove a result about monotonicity. Theorem. The function \(G(x)\) defined in equation (3) is increasing.

The ❌ version breaks a sentence across the theorem and starts the theorem with a symbol. The ✅ version uses a complete sentence, and the theorem names its object.




Write the statement of a theorem so that it stands alone. A reader who jumps to the theorem should not need the assumptions in the paragraph before it, so repeat them in the statement.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
section: 3 Display and number the formulas that matter
text:
3 Display and number the formulas that matter
Put each important formula on a line by itself. Number the important ones, even if you do not refer to them, because a reader may want to refer to them later. Quarto’s equation cross-references number a display and let you link to it.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
section: 4 Write numbers according to how they are used
text:
4 Write numbers according to how they are used
Spell out a small number when it is an adjective: “the proof uses three lemmas”. Write the numeral when the number is a name or a value: “Lemma 3 is used 12 times”, “the total rose by 4”. Capitalize the name of a numbered result, as in “Theorem 1” and “Lemma 2”.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
text:
5 Keep subscripts under control
Do not name the elements of a set unless you need to. If you write “Let \(X = \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}\)”, you will need \(x_{i_1}, \dots, x_{i_m}\) as soon as you take a subset of \(X\). A subscript on a subscript is hard to read. Write “an element \(x\) of \(X\)” instead, and refer to \(x\) and \(y\) for two elements. Use \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) only when you need two specified elements.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
section: 6 Choose the voice and the person
text:
6 Choose the voice and the person
Use “we” to mean the author and the reader together, as in “we can now prove”. Write “we prove”, not the passive “it can be proved”. Avoid “I” unless the author’s persona is relevant.
Write “assume that \(G\) is finite”, not “assume \(G\) is finite”. The word “that” helps the reader parse the sentence. Do not write “we have that \(y = z\)”; write “we have \(y = z\)”.

title: Writing mathematics in sentences
section: 7 Choose the proof that fits the claim
text:
7 Choose the proof that fits the claim
Do not use proof by contradiction where a direct proof will do. The course’s worked example proves a lemma both ways. The direct proof is shorter, and it does not assume that the entries are integers or restate their ordering.

title: Grammar
text:
NoteAI-Assisted Authorship



This chapter was written with the assistance of GitHub Copilot, which expanded on outlined ideas and draft notes provided by the author. The content represents the author’s perspective and has been reviewed for accuracy, but the detailed prose was generated through AI assistance.
Clear grammar removes friction between your ideas and your reader. This chapter collects a few grammatical habits that consistently make scientific writing easier to read.

title: Grammar
text:
1 Relative pronouns
Relative pronouns introduce a clause that describes a preceding noun. The relative pronouns are:

that
which
who
whom
whose

Two habits make these clauses easier to read: choosing between that and which correctly, and keeping the relative pronoun rather than dropping it.

1.1 Restrictive vs. non-restrictive clauses: that vs. which
Use that for a restrictive clause — one that identifies which thing you mean, and that cannot be removed without changing the meaning of the sentence. Use which, set off by commas, for a non-restrictive clause — one that adds information the reader does not need in order to know which thing you mean.







Example 1 (Restrictive clause (that))  

The dataset that we collected in 2023 contains 4,000 records.

The clause “that we collected in 2023” tells the reader which dataset we mean. Removing it changes the meaning, so the clause is restrictive and takes that with no comma.











Example 2 (Non-restrictive clause (which))  

Our 2023 dataset, which contains 4,000 records, is publicly available.

The clause “which contains 4,000 records” adds a detail, but the reader already knows which dataset we mean. The clause is non-restrictive, so it takes which and is set off by commas.




A quick test: if you can drop the clause without changing which thing you are describing, use which and commas; otherwise, use that.


1.2 Do not omit relative pronouns
English lets you drop a relative pronoun in some sentences, but keeping it makes the structure of the sentence explicit and easier to parse on the first read. Prefer to keep that, which, or who, even when the grammar would let you drop it.







Example 3 (Restoring an omitted relative pronoun)  

❌ This body of work laid the methodological groundwork I now apply to enteric fever.
✅ This body of work laid the methodological groundwork that I now apply to enteric fever.

The word “that” signals immediately that a describing clause is beginning, so the reader does not briefly misread “the methodological groundwork I” as a single phrase and then have to backtrack.

title: Grammar
text:
2 Demonstrative pronouns
There are four demonstrative words:

this
that
these
those

They can serve two roles. As adjectives, they modify a noun: “this result”, “those samples”. As standalone pronouns, they replace a noun: “This shows…”, “That means…”.
When a demonstrative stands alone as a pronoun, the reader has to search backward for its referent — and often the referent is a whole preceding clause rather than a single noun, which leaves the reference ambiguous. Prefer to follow a demonstrative with the noun it points to, so the reference is explicit. The adverbs here and there point the same way: “getting there” leaves the reader to guess where “there” is.
A demonstrative at the end of a sentence has no room after it for a naming noun, so a bare sentence-final this or that always leaves its referent unnamed. End the sentence with the noun instead.







Example 4 (Naming the referent)  

❌ The model overfit the training data. This poses a problem for deployment.
✅ The model overfit the training data. This overfitting poses a problem for deployment.
❌ The first model’s estimates were biased upward. The second model avoids this.
✅ The first model’s estimates were biased upward. The second model avoids this bias.

Adding the nouns “overfitting” and “bias” states exactly what each “this” refers to, instead of leaving the reader to infer it. The second pair ends its sentence with the demonstrative, so the fix has to add the noun after it, at the very end.

title: Grammar
text:
3 Quantifiers used as pronouns
Words that say how many, or how much, of something cause the same problem as demonstratives when they stand alone in place of a noun. Grammars call these words quantifiers, and call a quantifier that stands alone an indefinite pronoun. The common ones are:

both
all (and counted forms such as all three)
each
any
some
most
many
few
none

Every belongs to the same family, but it cannot stand alone (“every” needs a noun, as in “every model”), so it never causes this problem.
You do not need a complete list of quantifiers to apply the advice. Whenever a quantifier stands where a noun should be, the reader has to search backward to find out what it quantifies. Follow the quantifier with the noun: “both models”, “all three estimators”, “each interval”. An “of” phrase that names the noun works too: “none of the intervals”.







Example 5 (Naming what a quantifier refers to)  

❌ We fit a linear model and a spline model to the 2019 and 2020 surveys. Both return the same fit.
✅ We fit a linear model and a spline model to the 2019 and 2020 surveys. Both models return the same fit.

In the first version, “both” could mean the two models or the two surveys. Adding “models” settles which pair the sentence is about.

title: Grammar
text:
4 Avoid garden-path sentences
A garden-path sentence leads the reader into one reading and then forces them to go back and reread when the rest of the sentence does not fit (Wikipedia: Garden-path sentence). The sentence may be grammatical, but the reader parses it twice.
A common cause of garden-path sentences in technical writing is a clause that describes a noun but has lost its opening that or that were. Without the pronoun, the reader takes the noun and the start of the clause as one phrase and has to reattach the words that follow. Do not omit relative pronouns gives the general rule.
When you reread a sentence and stumble, find the point where your first reading went wrong, and rewrite the sentence so that the first reading is the right one.







Example 6 (Rewriting a garden-path sentence)  

❌ Report only SHAs a command you ran printed in full.
✅ Report only SHAs that appeared in full in the output of a command that you ran.

In the first version, the reader takes “SHAs a command you ran” as one phrase, then reaches “printed” and has to work out that “a command you ran printed in full” is a clause describing the SHAs. The rewrite marks the clause with “that” and keeps each verb next to its own subject.

title: Grammar
section: 5 Name the object of a relational noun
text:
5 Name the object of a relational noun
Some nouns name a relation, so they are incomplete without the thing they relate to. Relational nouns include:

cause (of what?)
effect (of what, on what?)
reason (for what?)
result (of what?)
example (of what?)

When one of these nouns appears without its “of” or “for” phrase, the reader has to recover the missing object from context, just as with a pronoun that has no clear referent. Write the object next to the noun.







Example 7 (Comparing four versions of one sentence) Each version tries to say what usually causes garden-path sentences.


A common cause in technical writing is a clause that describes a noun but has lost its opening that or that were.
In technical writing, a common cause is a clause that describes a noun but has lost its opening that or that were.
In technical writing, a common cause of garden-path parsing is a clause that describes a noun but has lost its opening that or that were.
A common cause of garden-path sentences in technical writing is a clause that describes a noun but has lost its opening that or that were.


Versions 1 and 2 never say what the clause causes, so the reader has to look back to find what “cause” refers to. Version 3 names the object, “garden-path parsing”, but its fronted phrase delays the subject (see Lead with the subject), and “garden-path parsing” introduces a second term for the “garden-path sentences” that the section defines. Version 4 names the object, uses the defined term, and starts with the subject.

title: Grammar
text:
6 Appositive fronting
An appositive is a noun phrase that renames or describes the noun beside it. In “Bovine respiratory disease (BRD), a disease complex with a multifactorial etiology, kills calves”, “a disease complex with a multifactorial etiology” is an appositive of “BRD”. Appositive fronting moves the appositive to the start of the sentence, before the noun it describes, which then follows as the subject: “A disease complex with a multifactorial etiology, BRD is a leading cause of mortality in calves.” Often the subject becomes a pronoun, as in “A disease complex with a multifactorial etiology, it is a leading cause of mortality in calves”, which needs an antecedent for “it” in the sentence before.
Fronting is a stylistic choice, with costs and benefits.
Benefits

It states the category before the specifics. The reader learns what kind of thing the subject is, then what is said about it.
It joins two statements without a connecting verb such as “is” or “serves as”, so the sentence is shorter.
It puts a familiar description first and the new claim last, where the reader’s attention lands.

Costs

The fronted phrase must describe the grammatical subject that follows. Otherwise it dangles: “A disease complex with a multifactorial etiology, mortality in calves is high” says that mortality is a disease complex.
The reader waits for the subject and verb, which runs against the advice to lead with the subject. A long fronted appositive delays them, and a reader may take the phrase for the subject (compare Avoid garden-path sentences).
The sentence no longer asserts the description as a main-clause claim, so the reader may treat it as background even when it is the point.
A pronoun subject (“it”) needs an antecedent in the previous sentence. A reader who cannot find it must stop to look.
It reads as more formal and literary, which suits some venues and not others.

Guideline. Front an appositive when it is short, familiar to the reader, and describes the subject. Keep the plain “X is Y” form when the description is the new information the paper depends on, when it is long, or when the subject is a pronoun without a clear antecedent.







Example 8 (Plain and fronted forms)  

Plain: Bovine respiratory disease (BRD) is a disease complex with a multifactorial etiology and serves as a significant cause of mortality among preweaned calves and weaned cattle alike.
Fronted: A disease complex with a multifactorial etiology, BRD is a leading cause of mortality in both preweaned calves and weaned cattle.

The fronted version is shorter and puts the category first. It works here because “a disease complex with a multifactorial etiology” describes BRD, the subject that follows it, and the subject is named, not a pronoun. If the multifactorial etiology is what the paper is about, the plain form states it as a claim the reader can challenge, and is the better choice.

title: Conciseness
text:
NoteAI-Assisted Authorship



This chapter was written with the assistance of GitHub Copilot, which expanded on outlined ideas and draft notes provided by the author. The content represents the author’s perspective and has been reviewed for accuracy, but the detailed prose was generated through AI assistance.
Concise writing conveys ideas efficiently, using only the words necessary to communicate meaning clearly. Every word should serve a purpose. Eliminate redundancy and verbosity. When you can express an idea in fewer words without losing meaning, do so.

title: Conciseness
text:
1 Common ways to improve conciseness

Remove redundant phrases

“in order to” → “to”
“due to the fact that” → “because”
“at this point in time” → “now”
“a large number of” → “many”

Use the active voice (see Write in the active voice)

“The experiment was conducted by the researchers” → “The researchers conducted the experiment”

Eliminate unnecessary qualifiers

“very”, “really”, “quite” often add little meaning

Replace wordy phrases with single words

“make a decision” → “decide”
“give consideration to” → “consider”
“is able to” → “can”


Remember: concise writing is not about making every sentence as short as possible, but about removing words that do not contribute to meaning or clarity. Keep a clause or a technical term when removing it would lose meaning or precision, and never replace an honest hedge with false confidence.

title: Conciseness
text:
2 Make every word tell
Strunk’s rule 13 states the principle: “Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences, for the same reason that a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts.” He adds that this “requires not that the writer make all his sentences short, or that he avoid all detail and treat his subjects only in outline, but that he make every word tell” (Strunk 1920, rule 13).
Strunk’s examples of expressions that waste words:

“the question as to whether” → “whether”
“used for fuel purposes” → “used for fuel”
“in a hasty manner” → “hastily”
“owing to the fact that” → “since”
“the fact that he had not succeeded” → “his failure”
“His brother, who is a member of the same firm” → “His brother, a member of the same firm”

The same rule applies to statistical writing: “We conducted an analysis of the data to determine whether there is an association between smoking and lung cancer” becomes “We tested whether smoking is associated with lung cancer”.

title: Conciseness
text:
3 Write in the active voice
Use the active voice unless you have a specific reason to use the passive. An active sentence names who did what, and it is usually shorter. A passive sentence can hide the actor, and the reader then has to guess who made the choice.
Choose the actor by who did the work:

Use “I” for what the author did, such as a choice the author made or a step in the author’s analysis. With several authors, use “we”.
Use “we” when the author and the reader work through an argument together, as in “we now compute the gradient”.


❌ The minimum was found exactly, and the model was chosen by eye.
✅ We found the minimum exactly, and we chose the model by eye. (The author and reader work through the example together.)
✅ I chose the model by eye, because the study had five points. (A single author reports a choice.)

Passive voice is the right choice in a few cases:

The actor is unknown or does not matter, as in “The samples were contaminated.”
The receiver of the action is the topic of the paragraph, and the sentence is easier to follow with it as the subject.
The actor would be a vague “someone” or “one”, and no real person or group acts.

When none of these applies, rewrite the sentence with an active verb.

title: Conciseness
section: 4 Write about the ideas, not the document
text:
4 Write about the ideas, not the document
A sentence about which part of the document holds a definition adds no content. State the idea and link the term, as Talk about the ideas, not the notes explains. The ✅ example below omits the link only because this guide has no page for the term.

❌ The statistics notes define the training error as the average loss on the fitted data.
✅ The training error is the average loss on the data used to fit the model.

title: Conciseness
text:
5 Lead with the subject
Start a sentence with its subject, not a dependent clause or a fronted phrase. A leading clause makes the reader hold a condition before knowing what it conditions.

❌ When the sample size grows, the estimate becomes more precise.
✅ The estimate becomes more precise as the sample size grows.

A fronted phrase delays the subject in the same way. Move a phrase such as “in technical writing” or “in this study” after the noun it limits, unless it sets a scope that the whole paragraph depends on.

❌ In technical writing, a common cause of garden-path sentences is a missing that.
✅ A common cause of garden-path sentences in technical writing is a missing that.

title: Conciseness
text:
6 Limit complex sentence structures
A sentence with several nested dependent clauses forces the reader to hold each unfinished clause in mind until the sentence finally resolves. Compound sentences joined by coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or) are usually fine, and an occasional dependent clause is fine too; the problem is piling several of them into a single sentence.
When a sentence becomes hard to follow, split it into shorter sentences, each carrying one main idea.







Example 1 (Splitting an over-nested sentence)  

❌ Because the assay, which we had validated the previous year using samples that were collected before the outbreak began, produced results that, although noisy, were consistent with prior reports, we proceeded with the analysis.
✅ We had validated the assay the previous year, using samples collected before the outbreak began. Its results were noisy but consistent with prior reports, so we proceeded with the analysis.

The revised version breaks one deeply nested sentence into two and restores the natural chronological order (validation, then results, then decision), so the reader can absorb each idea before moving on.

title: Conciseness
section: 7 Do not rule out readings no reader would make
text:
7 Do not rule out readings no reader would make
A definition says what a term means. It does not need to list the things the term does not mean, unless a reader is likely to confuse the two. A disclaimer against a reading nobody would make costs the reader a sentence and can plant the confusion it was meant to prevent.







Example 2 (Dropping a needless disclaimer)  

❌ In this manuscript, TTE means target trial emulation. It does not mean effect of treatment on the treated.
✅ In this manuscript, TTE means target trial emulation.

In causal inference, the average effect of treatment on the treated is usually abbreviated ATT, so a reader is unlikely to read “TTE” that way. The second sentence introduces a meaning that the reader would not otherwise have considered.




Keep a disclaimer when the confusion is real. For example, if “CI” could mean confidence interval or cumulative incidence in the same paper, say which one you mean each time.
The same test applies to explanations: explain what your intended readers do not already know, and leave out what they do. A methods section for statisticians does not need to define a p-value; a report for clinicians might.

title: Conciseness
text:
8 Avoid double negatives
A double negative states a claim by denying its opposite, as in these phrases:

“not uncommon”
“not unlikely”
“not inconsistent with”

The reader has to cancel the two negatives to recover the claim, and the result is often vaguer than the writer intended. State the claim directly. If you mean something weaker than the direct claim, say what the weaker claim is.
A single negative is fine. “We did not reject the null hypothesis” denies one thing, and it is the standard wording for a test result.







Example 3 (Stating a claim directly)  

❌ The association was not inconsistent with a dose-response relationship.
✅ The association was consistent with a dose-response relationship.
✅ The data do not rule out a dose-response relationship, but they do not support one either.

Writers usually choose “not inconsistent with” to hedge “consistent with”. The first rewrite drops the hedge; the second says what the hedge was for. Choose the one you mean.

title: Conciseness
section: 9 Write about the subject, not about the text
text:
9 Write about the subject, not about the text
Some sentences describe the document instead of its subject. They do one of these things:

announce that a point is coming;
rank a point;
comment on how a point changes what follows.

Each one makes the reader read a sentence before reaching the content it promises. State the content directly. Rhetorical reflexes lists related signpost phrases, such as “it is worth noting that”.







Example 4 (Replacing a sentence about the text)  

❌ One trap worth naming: the sample excludes people who moved.
✅ The sample excludes people who moved.
❌ The most important point is that the survey was voluntary.
✅ The survey was voluntary.
❌ One documented detail changes how the rest of this section reads: the survey was voluntary.
✅ The survey was voluntary, so the estimates apply only to people who chose to respond.

In the third pair, the rewrite states what the detail changes instead of saying that it changes something.

title: Conciseness
section: 10 Let a self-describing link stand alone
text:
10 Let a self-describing link stand alone
A URL often shows the name of what it points to and where that thing lives. When it does, do not also spell out that name or host around the link. The reader would read the same facts twice.







Example 5 (Dropping prose that repeats a URL)  

❌ For an example, see my public notes site Morrison-Lab/sds on GitHub (https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/sds).
✅ For an example, see https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/sds.

The URL already says that the site is on GitHub and that the repository is Morrison-Lab/sds.




Keep a descriptive label when the URL does not show what it points to, such as a DOI or a shortened link.

title: Conciseness
section: 11 Keep the writer out of the way
text:
11 Keep the writer out of the way
Mention yourself only where a sentence needs an actor, such as a request, an offer, or a decision you made. Elsewhere, make the subject of the sentence the thing the reader cares about. Extra references to the writer turn attention from the content to the person.







Example 6 (Moving the focus from the writer to the subject)  

❌ I tested this in a small private project, and I found that CI works well.
✅ CI works well in a small private test project.
❌ My build and review tools run on cloud services.
✅ The build and review tools run on cloud services.

A request still needs its actor: “Could the space be increased, or would you allow me to register my own runner?” keeps “me” because the request is about the writer’s runner.

title: Conciseness
text:
12 Do not overexplain
Say what the reader needs, and stop. Cut a qualifier, a restatement or a reason that the words before it already imply.







Example 7 (Cutting a clause the term already implies)  

❌ Estimated mean: the estimated value of the mean, whether or not it is a mean of an outcome.
✅ Estimated mean: the estimated value of the mean.

The first version adds a clause that “the mean” already covers. The second is complete.

title: Conciseness
text:
13 Put lists in bullet points
A list of three or more phrases, written inline and separated by commas, makes the reader count commas to find where each item ends. Write it as a bullet list instead, introduced by a sentence ending in a colon. Use a numbered list when the items are steps done in order.
A run of parallel sentences is a list too, even with only two items. The common case is a set of resources, such as videos or readings, where each sentence names one resource and links to it. Put each sentence in its own bullet, so the reader sees how many resources there are and where each one starts.
Bullet lists matter most on slides, where a reader scans a list rather than reading it as a sentence. The rule is one case of a broader preference for more structure: when content has a shape, show that shape in the markup.
A few mechanics to keep in mind when writing one:

Keep the items grammatically parallel, so each one completes the introducing sentence the same way.
Leave a blank line before the list; without it, Markdown reads the list as part of the paragraph above.
Keep a short series of single words inline, such as “R, Julia, or Python”.








Example 8 (Turning an inline list into bullet points)  

❌ Machine learning combines data to learn from, statistics to say what a finite sample of data supports, and optimization to find the model that fits the data best.
✅ Machine learning combines three components:

data to learn from;
statistics to say what a finite sample of data supports;
optimization to find the model that fits the data best.


The revised version puts each component on its own line, so the reader sees at a glance that there are three.











Example 9 (Turning a run of resource sentences into bullet points)  

❌ Hastie and Tibshirani extend least squares to several predictors. Starmer explains multiple regression.
✅ Videos:

Hastie and Tibshirani extend least squares to several predictors.
Starmer explains multiple regression.


For the video notes this example comes from, see the DATA 571 chapter on linear regression. Each bullet holds one video, so the reader can pick one without parsing the paragraph.











Example 10 (Turning inline steps into a numbered list)  

❌ k-means starts with \(k\) group centers, assigns each point to its nearest center, moves each center to the mean of its points, and repeats until the assignments stop changing.
✅ k-means starts with \(k\) group centers and repeats two steps until the assignments stop changing:

assign each point to its nearest center;
move each center to the mean of its points.


The numbers show the order of the steps, and the loop condition moves into the introducing sentence.

title: Conciseness
text:
14 Examples of concise writing
Many effective writers throughout history have exemplified the principle of conciseness.
Julius Caesar’s Commentarii and phrases like “Veni, vidi, vici” demonstrate the power of brevity (Wikipedia contributors 2026b).
Ernest Hemingway was known for his spare, direct prose style. His short sentences and simple words conveyed complex ideas and emotions without unnecessary embellishment (Wikipedia contributors 2026a).

title: Avoiding clichés
text:
NoteAI-Assisted Authorship



This chapter was written with the assistance of GitHub Copilot, which expanded on outlined ideas and draft notes provided by the author. The content represents the author’s perspective and has been reviewed for accuracy, but the detailed prose was generated through AI assistance.
Clichés recur across unrelated documents, so they make writing read as generic and unconsidered, even when the underlying content is sound.
AI writing assistants often produce these patterns in clusters, and many readers have learned to treat the patterns as signs that a draft was generated and to doubt that its author checked it.
Human drafts use the same patterns, so this chapter is for any writer, including anyone editing a draft that an assistant helped write. It catalogs the most common clichés so you can remove them.

title: Avoiding clichés
text:
1 Terms used in this chapter
The rest of this chapter uses these terms.







Definition 3 (Register) A writer’s register is the level of formality and kind of language they choose for a particular audience and setting, such as conversational, technical, or promotional.











Definition 4 (Antithesis) An antithesis is a construction that sets two contrasting ideas side by side in parallel form, such as “not X, but Y” or “X, not Y”.











Definition 5 (Hedge) A hedge is a word or phrase that softens a claim or marks uncertainty about it, such as “may”, “suggests”, or “possibly”.











Definition 6 (Copula) A copula is a verb, usually a form of “to be”, that links a subject to a description of it, as “is” does in “the estimate is biased”.











Definition 7 (Participial clause) A participial clause is a clause built on a verb form ending in “-ing” or “-ed” that has no subject of its own, such as “ensuring that the data are clean” at the end of a sentence.











Definition 8 (Aphorism) An aphorism is a short, quotable sentence that states a general truth or verdict.

title: Avoiding clichés
text:
2 A caveat
No single word or pattern below is wrong on its own. Each has legitimate uses. The signal is clustering and mechanical repetition, the same constructions appearing again and again regardless of what each sentence needs. Edit for the cluster, not the isolated instance, and do not flatten your prose into a voiceless register trying to avoid every word on a list.

title: Avoiding clichés
text:
3 Overused vocabulary
Some words turn up more often than needed, in stock prose and especially in machine-generated text. Many of them are also Latin-derived words with plainer alternatives, so the advice here overlaps with the Word choice chapter. Table 1 lists frequent offenders and plainer replacements.

Whole phrases recur too. “In today’s fast-paced world”, “it is important to note that”, and “plays a vital role in” add length without content; delete them and start with the actual point. Two more families recur, and each member should give way to the literal claim:

Stock metaphors:

“journey”
“pave the way”
“shed light on”
“at the heart of”
“sits at the intersection of”
“cornerstone”
“deep dive”, “dive into”

Stock framings:

“at its core”
“in essence”
“boils down to”
“when it comes to”
“in the realm of”
“the key takeaway”
“more than just”

title: Avoiding clichés
text:
4 Rhetorical reflexes
Writers reach for a few sentence shapes by reflex, whether or not the content calls for them.
The most recognizable is the not just X, but Y antithesis. It promises a profound contrast and usually delivers a hollow one.







Example 1 (The “not just X, but Y” reflex)  

❌ This method is not just fast — it is transformative.
✅ This method runs in half the time of the previous approach.

The plain version makes a concrete, verifiable claim. The antithesis frame makes none.




Other reflexes to watch for:

Mechanical lists of three. Three parallel items appear whether or not three is the right count. Use the number of items the point actually needs.
Signpost filler. Phrases like “it is worth noting that” and “importantly” announce a point instead of making it. Cut them and state the point directly.
Hedging stacks. “May potentially suggest” and “could possibly indicate” pile up qualifiers. Keep one honest hedge; drop the rest.
Hollow summaries. A closing paragraph that opens with “in conclusion” and only restates what you just said adds nothing. End on a real point.

title: Avoiding clichés
section: 5 Say what it is before what it is not
text:
5 Say what it is before what it is not
When a sentence needs both a positive claim and a denial, state the positive claim first. The reader learns what the subject is before being told what to rule out, and the denial then attaches to a claim already made. Opening with the denial makes the reader carry an unsupported denial until the second clause arrives.







Example 2 (Positive claim, then denial)  

❌ The padding is not a convention, it is an identity.
✅ The padding is an identity, not a convention.

The first version says “not a convention” before the reader knows what the padding is, then repeats the subject and verb to supply the claim. The second version states the claim once and ends on the contrast.
The order matters even when the sentence stays grammatical:

❌ The padding is not a convention but an identity.
✅ The padding is an identity, not a convention.

Both are correct sentences; the second puts the claim first. For the first pair, see the linear regression chapter of lds.




Often the denial can be cut. Keep it only when the reader might plausibly believe the rejected reading, as with a convention versus an identity. A denial that rejects a view nobody holds is the reframe (see Clichéd sentence shapes) in miniature: cut it and keep the claim.

title: Avoiding clichés
text:
6 Clichéd sentence shapes
Beyond the antithesis, clichéd drafts lean on a set of sentence shapes that stage a point instead of stating it.







Example 3 (A staged point)  

❌ It can read like a definition that says nothing. Its use is in what it forces you to name: a project that cannot say what its \(E\), \(T\) and \(P\) are has not yet stated a machine learning problem.
✅ A machine learning problem is stated only when its experience \(E\), task \(T\) and performance measure \(P\) are named.

The first version packs six clichés into two sentences:

an objection raised only to be knocked down;
“It” and “Its” in place of “the definition”;
a definition that “forces” the reader, as if it were a person;
“you” addressing the reader;
a point withheld until after a colon;
a closing aphorism.

The second version states the claim once.




Watch for these shapes:

The straw objection. A doubt raised only to be answered (“It may seem trivial. In fact, …”). This is the antithesis spread over two sentences.
The personified abstraction. A definition, method or result that “forces”, “invites”, “demands” or “asks” something of the reader. Name who does what.
The colon reveal. A setup, then a colon, then the point. Lead with the point.
