The answered rhetorical question. “The result? A faster fit.” or “Why does this matter? Because …”. State the result.
The throat-clearing lead-in. “Here’s the thing:”, “Here’s why:”, “The key is”, “Put simply,”. Delete the lead-in.
The announced claim. “It is what makes … valid”, “That is what …”, “This is what …”, and “What the standing grant removes is the need to ask”. The sentence points at its own claim before making it. Make the claim directly: “It is what makes sums over countably infinite partitions valid” becomes “It makes sums over countably infinite partitions valid”, and “What the standing grant removes is the need to ask” becomes “The standing grant removes the need to ask”. The same holds for a subject followed by “is what” and a verb, and for a tail of “, which is why” or “, which is what”: “The risk is what says how a model does on neighborhoods outside the sample” becomes “The risk measures how well a model predicts neighborhoods outside the sample”, “Solving the equation is what this course calls learning” becomes “This course calls solving the equation learning”, “No label was used, which is why the task is unsupervised” becomes “No label was used, so the task is unsupervised”, and “The step is cheap, which is what makes it affordable” becomes “The step is cheap, so it is affordable”. Keep a “, which is why” tail only where a real reason follows that the reader would not guess.
The reframe. “X isn’t about Y; it’s about Z”, “The question isn’t X, it’s Y”, and “not because X, but because Y”. Say what X is about.
Fragment emphasis. “Simple. Fast. Reliable.” Write a sentence with a subject and a verb.
The editorializing tail. A trailing participial clause that comments on the sentence: “, highlighting the importance of …”, “, ensuring that …”, “, making it ideal for …”. End the sentence at its claim.
The inflated copula. “Serves as”, “stands as” and “acts as” where “is” says the same.
The range frame. “From X to Y” listing two extremes instead of naming the scope.
The audience frame. “Whether you’re a student or a researcher, …”. Drop it.
The restatement. “In other words, …” repeating the previous sentence. Keep the clearer of the two.
The closing aphorism. A one-line verdict at the end of a paragraph: “And that’s the point.”, “Simple as that.”, “… has not yet stated a problem.” End on the last piece of content.
Sincerity intensifiers. “Genuinely”, “truly”, “actually”, “really” and “crucially” used to sound earnest. Cut them.
Chained connectors. “Furthermore”, “Moreover” and “Additionally” opening consecutive sentences. Most can go; the order already signals addition.
Assistant chatter. “Let’s dive in”, “Let’s unpack this”, “Great question” and “I hope this helps” belong in a chat window, not a document.

Four more habits blur the referent or delay the claim. Other chapters cover each:

a demonstrative standing in for its referent (Demonstrative pronouns);
the word “thing” (Say which thing);
a dependent clause opening a sentence (Lead with the subject);
informal idioms (Avoid vague and metaphorical language).

title: Avoiding clichés
text:
7 Formatting habits
Some clichés are typographic rather than verbal.

The em-dash as a default connector. Some writers, and many AI drafts, use the em-dash to join almost any two clauses. Vary your punctuation: a period, a comma, or a semicolon is often the better fit.
Bold-leading bullets everywhere. A **Term:** explanation bullet is fine once, but applying the pattern to every list turns it into a tic. Use it when the label earns emphasis, plain bullets otherwise.
Emoji section headers. Emoji in headings signal a blog post, not a scientific document. Leave them out.
Uniform paragraph rhythm. Paragraphs of near-identical length, each three or four sentences, read as monotonous. Let paragraph length follow the ideas.

title: Avoiding clichés
text:
8 Tone
The last group of clichés is about register.

Promotional language. Words like “powerful”, “game-changing”, and “cutting-edge” sell rather than inform. Describe what the thing does and let the reader judge.
Reflexive both-sides framing. Tacking “however, it is important to consider the other side” onto every claim signals caution without adding content. Use a hedge when the evidence is genuinely mixed, not by habit.
Vague universals. “Studies show” and “experts agree”, with no specific source or number, are clichés precisely because they dodge the evidence. Name the study and give the number, as the Citations and evidence chapter recommends.

title: Avoiding clichés
text:
9 How to use this list
Write plainly first, then scan the draft once before you share it. Use the same list when you review someone else’s writing.

One match means little. Several matches in one paragraph, or the same pattern repeated across a document, are the real signal.
Do not ban a word outright. Keep a word or phrase that is the precise one for the sentence.
Do not flatten your writing into a voiceless register. Cut the filler and the reflexes, and keep your own voice.
Skip the scan for code, terse status lines and short conversational replies.
Do not accuse a writer of using an assistant on the strength of the list. Say which pattern weakens the sentence and how to fix it.

title: Citations and evidence
text: Every claim in scientific writing should be supported by either citations to relevant sources or direct evidence from data or experiments. This principle is fundamental to maintaining credibility, enabling verification, and building on the accumulated knowledge of the scientific community.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
1 Why claims need support
Scientific writing aims to convey truthful, verifiable information. Unsupported claims undermine this goal in several ways:

Credibility: Readers cannot assess the reliability of assertions without knowing their basis
Verification: Claims without support cannot be independently verified or challenged
Reproducibility: Other researchers need sources to understand the foundation of your work
Intellectual honesty: Proper attribution gives credit where it is due and distinguishes your original contributions from existing knowledge
Learning pathway: Citations provide readers a roadmap to learn more about a topic

When you make a claim, you are asking readers to accept it as true. They deserve to know why they should trust that claim.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
2 What constitutes adequate support
Different types of claims require different types of support:

2.1 Empirical claims
Claims about observable phenomena or data should be supported by:

Direct presentation of the data (tables, figures, statistical analyses)
Citations to published studies that collected the relevant data
Description of experimental methods that generated the evidence
Links to publicly accessible datasets



2.2 Theoretical claims
Claims about concepts, models, or interpretations should be supported by:

Citations to papers that developed or validated the theory
Logical arguments with clearly stated premises
Mathematical derivations or proofs
References to review articles that synthesize relevant theoretical work



2.3 Methodological claims
Claims about appropriate methods or best practices should be supported by:

Citations to methodological papers or textbooks
Empirical evidence of method performance
Expert consensus statements
Validation studies



2.4 Common knowledge
Not every statement requires citation. Well-established facts that are common knowledge within your field (for example, “DNA is a double helix” in molecular biology) can be stated without citation. However, when in doubt, provide a citation—over-citing is preferable to under-citing.

title: Citations and evidence
section: 3 Do not substitute flippancy for support
text:
3 Do not substitute flippancy for support
Some phrases assert that a claim needs no support instead of supplying any:

“it is obvious that”
“clearly, it follows that”
“it should be familiar to you that”
“the familiar formula”
“of course”
“as everyone knows”

The problem is the appeal, not the individual words. “Clearly” is fine as an adverb of manner (“the methods section clearly describes the sampling frame”), and “of course” is fine when it flags an assumption you have already established. Each becomes a problem only when it stands in for an argument you have not made.
These phrases do no work for the reader. A reader who already knows the result gains nothing from being told that it is familiar, and a reader who does not is told that the gap is their own fault, without being given any way to close it. They also cost the writer something. Working a step out is how you find out whether it holds; calling it obvious settles the question by assertion, and leaves any error in the step where it is. So if you cannot supply a derivation or a citation for a step, treat that as a reason to work the step out, not as a reason to call it obvious.
Replace such phrases with one of the following:

A direct derivation. Show the intermediate steps, or state which identity or algebraic manipulation takes you from one line to the next.
A specific citation. Name the source that establishes the result, and give a chapter, section, page, or equation number whenever the source is long enough that a bare citation would leave the reader searching.
A cross-reference. When you established the result earlier in the same document, point to it by number (see Defining terms clearly for the Quarto cross-reference syntax).

Deleting the phrase and keeping the claim is also usually an improvement: “the log-likelihood is a sum of three terms” makes the same claim about the log-likelihood as “the log-likelihood is obviously a sum of three terms”, and it invites the reader to check the claim rather than to defer to it.







Example 1 (Replacing an appeal to familiarity)  

❌ Substituting the normal density into the likelihood gives the familiar three-term formula.
✅ For an independent sample \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) from a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), substituting the normal density into the likelihood and taking logarithms gives \[
\ell(\mu, \sigma^2) =
-\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi)
- \frac{n}{2}\log\left(\sigma^2\right)
- \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_i - \mu\right)^2.
\] The three terms are, in order:

a constant that does not involve the parameters;
a term that depends on \(\sigma^2\) but not on \(\mu\);
the sum of squared deviations of the data from \(\mu\), divided by \(-2\sigma^2\).


The second version gives the reader the formula and where it came from, so they can check the algebra themselves. The first version asks them to take the writer’s word for it, and offers no help to anyone who has not seen the result before.





3.1 “Trivial” and “trivially”
“Trivial” and “trivially” usually work the same way: they announce that a step is too small to write down, which relieves the writer of writing it down. Treat them as a prompt to check the step, and to write it out if it takes only a line.
The word has one defensible use, which is describing how a general expression reduces to a simpler one in a special case. For example, a weighted average reduces to an ordinary average when all of the weights are equal. Even in that use, “minimal case” or “degenerate case” names the situation more precisely, and avoids the dismissive tone that “trivial” carries.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
4 What makes a citation relevant
A relevant citation is one that actually supports the specific claim you are making. Common problems with citation relevance include:

Citing review papers indiscriminately: While review papers are valuable for general background, cite the original research when making specific claims about particular findings
Citing papers that don’t address the claim: Ensure the cited work actually discusses the point you’re making
Over-generalizing from narrow studies: Don’t cite a study with limited scope to support a broad general claim
Using outdated sources: When current knowledge has superseded older findings, cite more recent work

To ensure relevance:

Read the papers you cite (at least the relevant sections)
Verify that the cited work actually supports your specific claim
Cite the most direct source available
When citing for general background versus specific claims, make the distinction clear

title: Citations and evidence
text:
5 What makes a source trustworthy
Not all sources are equally reliable. Consider these factors when evaluating trustworthiness:

5.1 Peer review
Peer-reviewed publications in reputable journals have undergone expert scrutiny. This doesn’t guarantee correctness, but it provides a baseline level of quality control.


5.2 Reputation of authors and institutions
Work from recognized experts and well-regarded institutions tends to be more reliable, though this should not be the sole criterion.


5.3 Replication and consensus
Findings that have been replicated by independent groups or that represent scientific consensus are more trustworthy than isolated claims.


5.4 Transparency and reproducibility
Studies that:

Clearly describe their methods
Share their data and code
Disclose potential conflicts of interest
Have been successfully reproduced by others

are more trustworthy than those lacking these features.


5.5 Preprints and non-peer-reviewed sources
Preprints can be valuable for accessing cutting-edge research, but they have not undergone peer review. When citing preprints:

Note that they are preprints
Check whether a peer-reviewed version has since been published
Exercise extra scrutiny of the methods and conclusions



5.6 Sources to generally avoid
Some sources typically lack the rigor needed for scientific writing:

Wikipedia and general encyclopedias as the only source for a claim (cite them beside the primary source, as Cite Wikipedia, beside the primary source explains)
Popular press articles about scientific findings (cite the original research instead)
Blogs and social media posts (unless discussing public discourse or documenting specific claims made in those venues)
Predatory or pay-to-publish journals without genuine peer review
Retracted papers

title: Citations and evidence
text:
6 Copy-paste with caution
Copying exact wording — whether from another writer or from your own earlier work, and even with a citation — can cause problems: plagiarism, if the wording is not clearly marked as a quotation, and a shift in voice that makes the text harder to read.
A few rules of thumb:

Do not copy-paste prose from anyone who is not a coauthor of the document you are currently writing. If you must reproduce someone else’s exact words, mark them as a direct quotation and cite the source.
Prefer paraphrasing over quoting. Restating an idea in your own words, with a citation, usually reads better than a block quotation, and it shows that you understand the idea.
Do not recycle your own published text without thought. Reusing passages from your earlier papers (self-plagiarism) can violate journal policies; cite the earlier work instead of repeating it.

A related case is repetition within your own document. When a passage you are tempted to copy already appears elsewhere, cross-reference it instead of repeating it: this keeps a single source of truth and improves concision.

title: Citations and evidence
Citations and evidence
section: 8 Cite Wikipedia, beside the primary source
text:
8 Cite Wikipedia, beside the primary source
Wikipedia is free to every reader, and its articles on definitions, theorems and methods are usually reliable enough to orient a newcomer. So cite the Wikipedia article for each definition, theorem or named method whenever one exists: the citation gives readers a second, free presentation without leaving them to search for it.
The Wikipedia citation adds to the traditional reference and never replaces it. Cite it through the bibliography like any other source, with a @misc entry in references.bib (author {Wikipedia contributors}, the article’s URL, the access date) keyed wikipedia_<article_title>, and put the citation right after the content it covers, as [@wikipedia_poisson_distribution]. Keep the primary source’s citation beside the claim it supports. Never list a Wikipedia article in a Further reading section. Wikipedia appears only as a citation beside the content it covers. A Further reading section lists primary sources, textbooks, courses and other resources instead.

Cite the article for the specific concept, not a broader article that mentions it.
Read the article’s definition before citing it, because notation and conventions vary, and a reader who follows the link should find the same concept you defined. If the article’s convention differs from yours, say how.
Use a stable URL for the article, not a search result.
Cite an article once where its term is defined, not at every use; later uses link to your own definition.








Example 3 (Citing a definition’s Wikipedia article)  

❌ A Poisson random variable counts events in a fixed interval.
✅ A Poisson random variable counts events in a fixed interval (Wikipedia contributors 2026).

A reader who wants another presentation of the Poisson distribution now has one, and the definition itself still comes from your own text and its traditional reference.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
9 Number bracketed citations
On the lab’s notes sites, a bracketed citation, [@key], prints as a number, such as [1] or [1, p. 5]. An in-text citation, @key, prints the author name and the number, such as “Hastie et al. [2]”. Write [@key] when the source supports a claim, and @key when the author is the subject of the sentence. Never start a sentence or a list item with a bare @key unless the author is its subject. The author list becomes the subject, so a list of such items prints the same author name, such as “Wikipedia contributors [3]”, again and again. Write the description first, and end the sentence with the bracketed [@key]. The sites get this from the shared citation style and filter in Morrison-Lab/macros.

title: Citations and evidence
section: 10 Cite a source once per passage
text:
10 Cite a source once per passage
Cite a source once in each div or passage, at the claim it supports. A second citation of the same source in the same div adds a number that the reader must look up again and tells them nothing new. Cite again only when the second claim rests on a different part of the source, and then give a locator, such as [@key, p. 5]. The rule to cite a Wikipedia article once, where its term is defined, is a case of this one.







Example 4 (Citing one source once in a definition)  

❌ A Poisson random variable counts events in a fixed interval (Wikipedia contributors 2026). Source: Wikipedia contributors (2026).
✅ A Poisson random variable counts events in a fixed interval. Source: Wikipedia contributors (2026).

Both versions credit the same article. The second one does it once, in the source line that closes the div.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
11 Best practices
To effectively support your claims:

Cite as you write: Add citations immediately when making claims, rather than planning to “add references later”
Use citation management tools: Software like Zotero, Mendeley, or BibTeX helps organize and format references correctly
Check your citations: Before submitting, verify that every citation supports its associated claim
Provide context: Help readers understand why a source is relevant (for example, “Smith et al. (2020) demonstrated that…” rather than just “(Smith et al., 2020)”)
Balance primary and review sources: Use primary sources for specific findings, reviews for general background
Stay current: Supplement foundational older references with recent work showing the current state of knowledge
Cite diverse sources: When possible, include work from different research groups and perspectives

title: Citations and evidence
text:
12 Quote the original
Quote and cite the source that said it, not a later source that quotes it. Check the wording and the page against the original.

❌ Mitchell (1997), as quoted in Goodfellow et al. (2016), defines …
✅ “A computer program is said to learn …” (Mitchell 1997)

Credit a quotation to whoever speaks it in the primary source, even when the speaker is quoting someone else. When attribution is in doubt, read the primary source (a transcript, the original page) first. Uncertainty about who said a line is not evidence about who said it.

title: Citations and evidence
section: 13 Copy organization names from their source
text:
13 Copy organization names from their source
When a bibliography entry names an organization, copy the name from the organization’s own page (its about page, README or footer) rather than expanding an acronym from memory.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
14 Verify each bibliography entry
Check each detail of a bibliography entry against an official source. Look the work up through Crossref search or its REST API, check the title, volume, issue and pages against the record, and add the DOI. Check a constant in a cited theorem, such as the factors in an inequality, against a second free, official source, and say in the pull request what you checked against what.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
15 Cite an alias directly
When a source uses another name for a defined term, write the alias in bold and cite the source after it, as in also called the **alias** [@key, section]. The citation already says that the source uses the name, so do not add a sentence such as “The source uses that name”.

❌ also called the **alias**. The cited textbook uses that name.
✅ also called the **alias** [@key, section]

title: Citations and evidence
section: 16 Cite the original for named results

title: Citations and evidence
text:
17 Put the content first
Headings and sentences should name the topic, not its author: “A formal definition of machine learning”, not “Mitchell’s definition”. Follow a quotation with its citation alone, without commentary on who said it or where it was repeated.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
18 Adapting another course’s material
When teaching material draws on another course, write your own version of the content rather than summarizing how that course presents it. Credit the source in a note at the start or end of the adapted section.
Put that note in a div, never in running prose. An attribution is not part of the argument, and a reader skimming the section should be able to tell it apart from the content it credits. In Quarto, use a collapsed .callout-note titled “Source”, which frames the credit and keeps it out of the way on the page. A ::: notes div keeps the credit out of the slides, but on an HTML page it renders as a plain unstyled <div>, which looks like running prose; use it only on a site whose stylesheet sets .notes apart.
The same applies to license notices and to statements of how the adaptation differs from the source.
❌ A plain paragraph between the heading and the first definition:
This section is adapted from @zhou2024, used under the MIT License.
✅ The same credit in a collapsed callout:
::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Source

This section is adapted from @zhou2024, used under the MIT License.
:::

title: Citations and evidence
text:
19 Material from your own work
Do not formally acknowledge material you borrow from yourself or your own group. “Your group” means you and the other members of the labs that maintain the work, such as the Morrison Lab and UCD-SERG. Link to it, but do not credit it, except for the credits and citations listed below. This covers:

Material your group wrote that moves between repositories you maintain. When lecture notes move from one course repository to another, leave the sister-repository credit out of the new work. Material in those repositories that someone outside the group wrote keeps its credit (see below).
Text, figures or code reused from work that you or your group wrote elsewhere, such as a lab manual your group maintains (the UCD-SERG lab manual, for example), your own papers, or your own software.
A template or tool of your group’s that you built the site from.

A formal acknowledgment tells the reader the material came from someone else, so it does not belong on material that is your own, wherever that material is stored. A co-author outside your group is someone else: when you reuse a co-written paper or manual, the work itself gets no credit (a publisher-required citation aside, see below), but credit each outside co-author by name, in a sentence or an author line. The rule concerns acknowledging reuse of your own material. Citing a published paper or released software of yours as the original publication of a result, or as a tool you used, is ordinary citation and stays. A passage or figure reused from a published paper of yours follows the publisher’s reuse terms, which may require a citation; that is the only citation the reuse itself can require.
Do not cite your own course notes or sites as the source of a definition or result either. Instead, cite the original publication where you can identify one, and a modern textbook (see Cite the original for named results), and link to your own page as further reading.
❌ A citation of the group’s own notes as the source of a definition:
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds the inner product by the product of the norms [@morrison2026mds].
✅ The original source and a textbook, with a cross-reference link to the group’s page:
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality bounds the inner product by the product of the norms [@original, sec. 2; @textbook, ch. 3].
See also the
[Cauchy-Schwarz inequality](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/linear-algebra-inner-products.html#thm-cauchy-schwarz)
in the sister notes.
Carry over what the source of your material itself credits:

A book, paper or other work the material follows. For example, the Benjamin-Chung Lab Manual, which the UCD-SERG manual credits.
A person outside your group whose lecture or notes that source adapted, credited by name. For example, the lds course credits Kameron Decker Harris, Brian Hutchinson and Logan Sizemore, so any repository that reuses those lectures credits them too.

A link to a sister site that sends the reader to further reading is a cross-reference, not an attribution, so it stays.
When you find an existing credit to your own work, remove it and add or keep a link to it.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
20 Common citation errors to avoid

Citation needed: Making claims without any supporting citation or evidence
Vague attribution: Using phrases like “studies have shown” without citing specific studies
Appeal to obviousness: Using “obviously”, “clearly”, or “as everyone knows” in place of a derivation or a citation
Circular citation: Citing a paper that doesn’t contain the claimed information but cites another paper that does (cite the original source)
Redundant citation: Citing the same source more than once in one div or passage (see Cite a source once per passage)
Citation padding: Adding citations that don’t actually support your claims just to appear well-referenced
Selective citation: Only citing work that supports your position while ignoring contradictory evidence
Ghost authorship: Failing to cite work that directly influenced your ideas

title: Citations and evidence
text:
21 Examples

21.1 Poor (unsupported claim)

Machine learning models often perform poorly on small datasets.

Problem: This claim is stated as fact without any support.


21.2 Better (citation provided)

Machine learning models often perform poorly on small datasets (Vapnik 1998; Hawkins 2004).

Improvement: Citations provide evidence for the claim.


21.3 Best (citation with context)

Machine learning models often perform poorly on small datasets. Vapnik (1998) showed that the generalization error of learning algorithms typically decreases as training set size increases, and Hawkins (2004) demonstrated that complex models are particularly prone to overfitting when trained on limited data (Vapnik 1998; Hawkins 2004).

Improvement: The specific support each citation provides is explained.


21.4 Poor (irrelevant citation)

Python is the most popular programming language for data science (Knuth 1984).

Problem: Knuth’s 1984 paper on literate programming doesn’t address Python or data science.


21.5 Better (relevant citation)

Python is the most popular programming language for data science (Stack Overflow 2024).

Improvement: The citation is to a current survey of programming language usage.

title: Citations and evidence
text:
22 Conclusion
Supporting claims with appropriate citations and evidence is not optional—it is essential to scientific communication. It allows readers to verify your claims, understand the foundation of your arguments, and locate resources for further learning. Always ask yourself: “How does my reader know this is true?” If your text does not answer that question, add a citation or present direct evidence.

title: Defining terms clearly
text: Clear definitions are essential to effective scientific writing. Every specialized term should have an explicit, concise definition before its first use. Readers should not need to search for the meaning of a term or infer it from context alone. For example:

title: Defining terms clearly
text:
1 Guidelines for defining terms
Follow these principles when introducing new terms:

Provide explicit definitions: State clearly what a term means, rather than assuming readers will understand from context.
Be concise: Definitions should be brief and focused, using only the words necessary to convey the meaning. A definition block holds the defining statement and nothing else: no examples, special cases, motivation or caveats.
State technical definitions and results in both prose and a display equation: Give a quantitative term, or a theorem or corollary, a one-sentence prose statement and the formula it stands for as a display equation, in the same definition or theorem block; together the sentence and the formula are the statement. A formula left inline in the sentence is easy to miss and hard for later derivations to point to. The prose tells the reader what the quantity means; the formula makes it exact and lets later derivations cite it. For example, define the ordinary least squares estimate of a parameter vector \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\theta}}\vphantom{\theta}}\) as “the value of \(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\theta}}\vphantom{\theta}}\) that minimizes the residual sum of squares” and as
\[\hat{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\theta}}\vphantom{\theta}}} := \arg\min_{\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\theta}}\vphantom{\theta}}} \text{RSS}(\mathord{\smash[b]{\underset{\raise.3ex\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}}{\theta}}\vphantom{\theta}}),\]
not with only one of the two. Build the formula from terms already defined, rather than expanding them again: once the residual and total sums of squares are defined, write
\[R^2 := 1 - \frac{\text{RSS}}{\text{TSS}},\]
not the two sums that RSS and TSS stand for.
Define a statistical model by its distribution, and derive its other forms: Define a regression model by the distribution of the outcome conditional on the covariates, centered on a named mean function. For example, define simple linear regression as \(Y_i \mid X_i = x_i \sim \text{N}(\mu_i, \sigma^2)\), independently, with \(\mu_i := \mu(x_i)\) and \(\mu(x) := \beta_0 + \beta_x x\). Then define the deviation \(\varepsilon_i := Y_i - \mu(x_i)\), and state \(Y_i = \mu_i + \varepsilon_i\) with \(\varepsilon_i \mid X_i = x_i \sim \text{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) as a result proved from those definitions. Writing the model as “\(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_x x_i + \varepsilon_i\) with Gaussian errors” makes the definition rest on a quantity that has not been defined yet, and hides that the model is a statement about the outcome’s distribution.
Define a probability distribution by its density or mass function: Define a named distribution directly, by its probability density function (pdf) or probability mass function (pmf) and its support. State any relationship to other distributions as a theorem proved from those definitions. For example, define the chi-square distribution with \(k\) degrees of freedom by its pdf
\[f(x) := \frac{x^{k/2 - 1} e^{-x/2}}{2^{k/2}\,\Gamma(k/2)}, \quad x \in (0, \infty),\]
and state as a theorem that, for a positive integer \(k\), the sum of the squares of \(k\) independent standard normal random variables has this distribution. The density is defined for every real \(k > 0\); the theorem covers only integer \(k\). Defining the chi-square distribution as that sum turns a result into a definition, and leaves the reader without the density that later calculations need.
Define a term directly, not as a modification of another term: State what the term is, in its own words and symbols. Do not make the reader recall a different term and then apply a list of changes to it. For example, define the expected prediction error as the population mean of the squared prediction error over training sets and new observations, rather than as “the sample mean squared error of predictions, with the average over observations replaced by an expectation”. The second wording makes the reader build a term that the definition then discards. Link a related term when it helps, and relate the two in an example or a remark after the definition.
Define in the most general form the document needs: State the concept at the level of generality the rest of the document relies on, not just for the first case the reader meets. For example, define the residual sum of squares as the sum of squared residuals of any fitted model, not as a formula for a straight line. A definition tied to one special case has to be restated, or silently stretched, the first time the document needs the general case.
Follow the definition with examples, from general to specific: Put each special case in its own example block right after the definition, ordered from the most general to the most specific, each linking back to the definition or to the example it specializes (see Order: general definition, then examples).
Define terms at first use: Place the definition of a term before the first definition, theorem or passage that relies on it, so that every link to a definition points backward rather than forward (see Avoid forward references). When a definition or theorem uses a term whose definition comes later in the document, reorder the content so the definition comes first; do not remove the hyperlink to hide the forward reference.
Give every key term a formal definition in a #def- div: A term that the document relies on needs its own definition div, even if an exercise, a solution, an example or a sentence of prose has already explained it. An explanation inside an exercise or solution cannot be linked to as a definition, and a student who skips the exercise never sees it. Find the gaps by listing the terms the document uses, such as the bolded phrases and the terms in section titles, and checking that each one has a #def- div, or a link to the page that has one. This extends Give each term its own definition block below from terms defined in passing to terms explained only in exercises. For example, if “loss function” first appears in an exercise that asks students to compute one, add a #def-loss-function div before the exercise, and link the exercise’s mentions to it.
Pair each technical term with its mathematical symbol: Whenever a definition, an example or a list names a quantity in words, write its symbol beside the name. For example, write “the slope \(\beta_x\)” and “the residual sum of squares \(\text{RSS}\)”, not “the slope” and “the residual sum of squares” alone. The words tell the reader what the quantity means, and the symbol tells the reader which letters stand for it in the equations that follow.
Define and link every technical term at its first use in each div: Inside a definition, theorem, example or other div, link a technical term to its formal definition the first time it appears in that div. Outside divs, link it the first time it appears in each prose passage. A link in an earlier div does not carry over, because readers jump into the middle of a page. Link once per div or passage, not at every mention. If the term has no formal definition yet, write the definition in its own definition div, then link to it. Never define a term inline inside another div, because an inline definition cannot be linked to from anywhere else. In a series of related documents, such as course notes, first look for a definition in an earlier document and link to it if one exists. Otherwise write the definition in the earliest document that needs the term. A passage is the prose outside divs between one heading and the next, and each div counts separately from the passage around it and from every other div. For example, if a div defines noise as the outcome minus the “true function”, link the term as [true function](#def-true-function), and first add a definition div with that ID if the document lacks one. A counterexample: the definition of noise links “mean”. The example block after it also uses “mean”, but without a link, wrongly assuming the earlier link carries over. The example block should link “mean” at its own first use.
Do not presuppose what the reader has not met: A definite noun phrase, one that starts with “the”, presupposes that the reader already knows what it refers to. “Fit a line to the synthetic data” is unjustified if no earlier sentence has said which data these are, or where they came from. Check each “the …” phrase for a referent the reader has already seen. If there is none, introduce the referent first, or write “a” or “some” in place of “the”. Then link each definite noun phrase to what it refers to, with a cross-reference such as [the synthetic data](#exm-synthetic-data), so that a reader who has forgotten or skipped the referent can find it. Skip the link when the referent is introduced in the same div, or in the same prose passage, as the phrase. Inside a div, the antecedent has to be in that div: an earlier div does not count, because readers jump into the middle of a page. For example, an exercise that says “Explain the labels” with no labels named in it has no antecedent, even if an earlier exercise names some. Name the labels in the exercise, or link them to where they are introduced.
Provide examples and counterexamples: Every definition should include at least one concrete example that illustrates how the term is used, and at least one counterexample: a case that looks as if it fits the definition but does not. The example shows what the term covers; the counterexample shows where its boundary is, which is often where readers misapply it. Put each in its own example block after the definition.
Give each term its own definition block: In a Quarto document, put every definition in its own #def- div (see Using theorem environments in Quarto), one term per div, with commentary after the div rather than inside it, in a remark block (#rem-) when it is about the concept. Never nest one theorem-type block (any of the prefixes listed in Using theorem environments in Quarto, such as #def-, #exm-, #exr-, #sol- or #rem-) inside another; give each its own div, in order. A bolded term in running prose is usually an inline definition that belongs in a div, including a term defined in passing. Give closely related terms separate divs too: only full synonyms share one (see Name the synonyms below). For example, the left and right distributive laws are two properties, each with its own identifier, example and exercise, so define them in two divs. A reader who needs one of them can then link to exactly that one.







Example 5 (Splitting two related definitions)  

❌ Definition (distributive laws). Multiplication distributes over addition on the left if \(a(b + c) = ab + ac\) and on the right if \((a + b)c = ac + bc\).
✅ Definition (left distributivity). Multiplication distributes over addition on the left if \(a(b + c) = ab + ac\) for all \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\).
✅ Definition (right distributivity). Multiplication distributes over addition on the right if \((a + b)c = ac + bc\) for all \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\).

The first block cannot be linked to as “left distributivity” without also pointing at the other law, and one example cannot illustrate both. For numbers, right distributivity follows from left distributivity because multiplication commutes, so one example checks both. Matrix multiplication does not commute, so establishing one law does not establish the other, and each needs its own example.




Name the synonyms: When a field uses several words for one concept, such as learning, training and fitting a model, every word that names the concept is an alternative name, and each is treated exactly as the primary name: put all of them in the div title, as in “Postulate (axiom)”, and bold each where it first appears in the definition. This covers the names other sources use, such as a textbook’s, which belong in the title and in bold too, as in “Risk (expected loss, population risk, true risk, generalization error, expected prediction error)”. Say which one the document uses. Name near-synonyms in the definition block or in a callout beside it, and state how they differ. A reader who meets the other words in another source can then connect them to the concept already learned (see Minimize unnecessary jargon).
Distinguish estimands from estimators: An estimand is the quantity a study is after, defined on the population or the data-generating distribution; an estimator is the rule that computes an estimate of it from a sample. Define a quantity first as its estimand, then give the estimator that targets it, and keep the two in separate notation (for example, \(\theta\) and \(\hat\theta\)). A definition that gives only the sample formula hides what the formula estimates, and invites the reader to treat one sample’s value as the quantity itself. Keep that order across the whole document, not only within one definition: the estimand’s definition, with its exercise and example, comes before the estimator’s, and the estimator’s definition links back to it. For example, define the risk of a model, its expected loss on new data, before the empirical risk, its average loss on the training data; define the population mean before the sample mean, and a parameter before its maximum likelihood estimate. Reading the estimator first leaves the reader with a formula and no answer to the question of what it is for. When several related quantities are defined together, give a table with one row per quantity and a column each for its name, its estimand and its estimator. For a binary classifier with prediction \(\hat Y\) of the true class \(Y\), and counts \(\text{TP}\), \(\text{FP}\), \(\text{FN}\) and \(\text{TN}\) from a test set of size \(n\):








Name
Estimand
Estimator




Accuracy
\(\Pr(\hat Y = Y)\)
\((\text{TP} + \text{TN}) / n\)


Precision
\(\Pr(Y = 1 \mid \hat Y = 1)\)
\(\text{TP} / (\text{TP} + \text{FP})\)


Recall
\(\Pr(\hat Y = 1 \mid Y = 1)\)
\(\text{TP} / (\text{TP} + \text{FN})\)



The precision of a classifier is a property of the classifier and the population it is used on; \(\text{TP} / (\text{TP} + \text{FP})\) is one test set’s estimate of it.
Name the target of every estimator and predictor: Every estimator has one target estimand, and the definition says which. A prediction is not an estimator of a mean. Its estimand is the observed outcome value of a new data point, not the population mean of that outcome. For example, the fitted model at \(x\) is an estimator of the mean function value \(\mu(x)\), so its bias is measured against that mean, while the prediction at \(x\) has the new outcome \(Y_{*}\) as its estimand, so its prediction error is measured against \(Y_{*}\). Write “the fitted model at \(x\) as an estimator of the mean function value”, or “the prediction of the new outcome”, and never leave the target implicit.
Say which error: A bare “error” does not say what is measured, on which data, or whether it is a value computed from one sample or an expectation. Every use of “error” (and of “loss”) names three things: the quantity measured, such as the squared prediction error; the data that it is computed on, such as the training set, the validation set, the test set or the population; and whether it is a sample value or an expectation. For example, write “the prediction error on the validation set”, or “the expected squared prediction error”, and never “the error” or “the smallest error”. A term that already carries all three, such as the generalization error, can stand alone after its definition.
Make the fitted model the subject, not the fitting procedure: A prediction, an error, a bias and a variance are all properties of fitted models, so a sentence about them has a fitted model as its subject, and a choice among candidates is a choice among fitted models. Write “the fitted model predicts”, “the prediction of the fitted model at \(x\)”, and “choose among fitted models”, and never “the procedure predicts” or “choose among procedures”. Name the fitting procedure only when the sentence is about how a fitted model is built: the inputs that the procedure needs, what it costs, or an expectation over the training sets to which it is applied. In math, write \({\hat y_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}}\) for the fitted model, the model that the procedure produces from the training set, and \(g\) only for the procedure itself. Where the training set is not salient, write the fitted model as \(\hat y\) instead, the symbol that the predicted-value bullet below builds on. For example, write “the bias of the prediction \(\hat{y}\)”, not “the bias of \(g\)”.
Say “fitted model”, not “prediction rule”: A fitted model that is used to predict outcomes is still a fitted model, and a second name for one object makes readers wonder whether there are two objects, so call it a fitted model every time. Write “the fitted model predicts”, and never “the prediction rule predicts”. When a set of notes defines the fitted model, “prediction rule” belongs only in that definition, as an alias in bold and in the div title, so that a reader who meets the alias elsewhere can find its meaning. If the notes once defined “prediction rule” under its own anchor, keep the old anchor as a span on the alias, so that links to it still land there.
Write a predicted value with the predicted-value macro: A predicted value is the fitted model applied to a covariate value, so write it with a predicted-value macro and not as the procedure applied to a covariate value and a training set. The macro \predval takes no argument and prints the predicted value of the outcome at the covariate value that the sentence is about. The macro \predvalf{x} takes a covariate value \(x\) and prints the prediction \(\hat y\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}\), a value of the outcome’s type. The macro \candpredvalf{l}{x} takes a candidate index \(l\) and a covariate value \(x\), and prints the prediction of candidate \(l\)’s fitted model at \(x\). Suppress the covariate value where it is not salient: write \predval when the sentence is not about which covariate value the prediction is at, and \predvalf or \candpredvalf only when the covariate value matters, such as when comparing predictions at two covariate values or averaging a prediction over them. For example, write \(\hat{y}\) in “the bias of the prediction \(\hat{y}\)” when one covariate value is fixed throughout, write \({\hat y\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\) and \({{\hat y_{l}}\mathopen{}\left(x\right)\mathclose{}}\) when the covariate value is salient, and never \(g\mathopen{}\left(x; \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\right)\mathclose{}\) or \(g_{l}\mathopen{}\left(x; \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\right)\mathclose{}\).
Apply a function to its argument with the macro’s f form: Where a macro names a function, such as a fitting procedure, the macro with an f ending applies it to its argument, so write the application with that macro and not with a hand-typed \paren. For example, write \(g\mathopen{}\left(\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\right)\mathclose{}\) for the fitted model that \(g\) gives on the training set \(\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\), and never \(g\mathopen{}\left(\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\right)\mathclose{}\). The same holds for an operator and every delimiter macro (\paren, \sb, \cb, \set, \abs, \norm and \angb), and for an alias of the operator: write \(\operatorname{E}\mathopen{}\left[y\right]\mathclose{}\), and never \(\operatorname{E}\mathopen{}\left[y\right]\mathclose{}\). Before adding an f form, check that no macro already prints the notation: \candfitted{l} already prints the fitted model of candidate \(l\), and a second macro for the same notation is not an f form. When no macro prints the notation, create the f form in the macros repository first, in the same session, then bump the pin and use it, as for any new macro. A missing f form is never a reason to type the operator and the delimiter separately.
Qualify “mean”, “average” and their shorthands as population or sample: A bare “mean” or “average” does not say whether it is a quantity of the population or a value computed from one sample. Write “population mean” for the expected value of a distribution, and “sample mean” for the average of the observed values; write “population average” and “sample average” in the same way. Prefer “mean” with the qualifier to “average”. The same holds for shorthands: write pMSE and sMSE, pRMSE and sRMSE, and pMAE and sMAE, with a leading p for the population version and s for the sample version, and never a bare MSE, RMSE or MAE. Spelled out, the same words apply: “population mean squared error”, “sample root mean squared error”, “population mean absolute error”. Define each shorthand once, at first use, as “population mean squared error (pMSE)”. A term that already says which, such as “mean function” or “running mean”, needs no extra word, and neither does expected value notation such as \(\operatorname{E}\mathopen{}\left[Y\right]\mathclose{}\). For example, write “the sample mean of the training outcomes estimates the population mean of the outcome”, not “the mean estimates the mean”. Drop the qualifier only when it is completely clear from context, such as inside a definition that has just said which one it concerns. When in doubt, keep it.

title: Defining terms clearly
text:
2 Examples of term definitions
Here are examples of well-defined terms:







Definition 3 (Confidence interval) A confidence interval with confidence level \(1 - \alpha\) for a parameter \(\theta\) is an interval \([L, U]\) computed from a sample that contains \(\theta\) with probability \(1 - \alpha\) over repeated samples:
\[\Pr(\theta \in [L, U]) = 1 - \alpha.\]











Example 6 (A confidence interval for mean height) If we calculate a 95% confidence interval (Definition 3) for mean height as [165 cm, 175 cm], we are 95% confident that the true population mean height falls within this range.











Example 7 (A range that is not a confidence interval for the mean) The interval from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile of the observed heights, [150 cm, 190 cm], is not a 95% confidence interval (Definition 3) for mean height. The percentile interval describes where individual heights fall, not where the population mean is likely to be, and it does not shrink as the sample grows.











Definition 4 (Active voice) Active voice is a sentence structure where the subject performs the action expressed by the verb.











Example 8 (A sentence in active voice) “The researcher conducted the experiment” is in active voice (Definition 4): the subject, “the researcher”, performs the action, “conducted”.











Example 9 (A sentence that is not in active voice) “The experiment was conducted by the researcher” is not in active voice (Definition 4). Its subject, “the experiment”, receives the action instead of performing it, so the sentence is in passive voice.

title: Defining terms clearly
text:
3 Order: general definition, then examples
When a concept has special cases, write the general definition first and compactly, then one example block per special case, ordered from the most general to the most specific. Put any commentary in a remark block after them. When the special cases have their own definitions, define the general concept first from prerequisite terms defined before it, and then define the special cases after it. Do not define the general concept by listing the special-case definitions that follow it, or move the general definition after its special cases: define the prerequisite terms first (for example, define lower and upper bounds first, then define an interval as a subset of the real numbers between two bounds, possibly including one or both bounds, and then define closed, open and half-open intervals). For example, a statistics text that defines the residual sum of squares would give these blocks, in this order:







Definition 5 (Residual sum of squares) The residual sum of squares of a model fitted to data is the sum of its squared residuals:
\[\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n r_i^2.\]











Example 10 (Residual sum of squares of a straight line) For a straight line with intercept \(\beta_0\) and slope \(\beta_x\), the fitted value of observation \(i\) is \(\beta_0 + \beta_x x_i\), so the residual sum of squares (Definition 5) is a function of the two coefficients:
\[
\text{RSS}(\beta_0, \beta_x) = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_x x_i)^2.
\]











Example 11 (Residual sum of squares of a line through three points) For the points \((0, 1)\), \((1, 2)\), \((2, 2)\) and the line with \(\beta_0 = 1\) and \(\beta_x = 0.5\) (Example 10), the residuals are \(0\), \(0.5\) and \(0\), so \(\text{RSS}(1, 0.5) = 0.25\).











Example 12 (A sum of squares that is not a residual sum of squares) For the same three points, the sum of squared deviations of \(y_i\) from their mean, \(5/3\), is \(2/3\). That quantity is the total sum of squares, not the residual sum of squares (Definition 5) of the line in Example 11, because it measures spread around the mean rather than around the line’s fitted values.




The definition stays one sentence and one equation, so it still applies when the document later fits a model that is not a line. The line is a special case, so it is an example, and the numerical case is a special case of the line, so it follows the line. The counterexample comes after the examples, once the reader knows what the definition covers.

title: Defining terms clearly
section: 4 Give a defined quantity its expression and its prose reading
text:
4 Give a defined quantity its expression and its prose reading
When a term names a quantity with a mathematical form, the definition states the expression and then reads it aloud in a prose sentence that says the same thing. The expression makes the definition exact. The prose reading lets the reader check that they understood it. The two must match (see Make the prose say what the formula says). A term with no mathematical form, such as active voice, keeps its prose definition alone.







Definition 6 (Variance, with its expression and its prose reading) The variance of a random variable \(X\) is \[\operatorname{Var}\mathopen{}\left(X\right)\mathclose{} = \operatorname{E}\mathopen{}\left[\mathopen{}\left(X - \operatorname{E}\mathopen{}\left[X\right]\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}^2\right]\mathclose{}.\] In words, it is the population mean of the squared deviation of \(X\) from its population mean.











Example 13 (A definition that gives only one of the two) “The variance is how spread out \(X\) is” gives no expression, so a reader cannot compute it. “The variance is \(\operatorname{E}\mathopen{}\left[\mathopen{}\left(X - \operatorname{E}\mathopen{}\left[X\right]\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}^2\right]\mathclose{}\)” gives no reading, so a reader cannot check their understanding. Definition 6 gives both.

title: Defining terms clearly
text:
5 Why examples matter
Examples serve several crucial purposes:

Concrete understanding: Examples transform abstract concepts into tangible instances that readers can visualize and understand.
Verification: Readers can work through examples themselves to verify they understand the definition or theorem.
Application: Examples show how to apply definitions and theorems to solve real problems.
Memory: Concrete examples are easier to remember than abstract definitions alone.
Boundaries: Counterexamples show where a definition stops applying, which is where readers most often misapply it.

title: Defining terms clearly
text:
6 Common pitfalls to avoid

Circular definitions: Do not define a term using the term itself.
Incorrect: “Conciseness is the quality of being concise.”
Correct: “Conciseness is the quality of expressing ideas using only the words necessary to communicate meaning clearly.”
Qualifying the term does not make the definition less circular. “A new observation relative to a training set is a new observation when …” still uses the term in its own definition. Define it directly instead: “A new observation relative to a training set is a covariate value and an outcome drawn from the same population as the training observations and independent of them.”
Vague definitions: Avoid definitions that rely on imprecise language.
Incorrect: “A variable is something that can change.”
Correct: “A variable is a symbol representing a value that can take on different values.”
Missing examples: Never leave a definition without at least one example.
Examples without context: Ensure examples clearly illustrate the specific aspect of the definition they are meant to demonstrate.

title: Defining terms clearly
text:
7 Mathematical statements require examples
Mathematical theorems, lemmas, corollaries, and postulates should always include examples that demonstrate their application. Abstract mathematical statements become more accessible when readers can see concrete instances.

7.1 Using theorem environments in Quarto
When writing mathematical or technical content in Quarto, use theorem environments to demarcate and highlight the structure of your content. These environments provide consistent formatting, automatic numbering, and cross-reference capabilities.
Quarto provides built-in theorem environments including:

#thm- for theorems
#lem- for lemmas
#cor- for corollaries
#prp- for propositions
#cnj- for conjectures
#def- for definitions
#exm- for examples
#exr- for exercises
#sol- for solutions, named after their exercise (#exr-foo and #sol-foo)
#rem- for remarks

See the Quarto documentation on theorems and proofs for complete details.
Example syntax:
::: {#thm-pythagorean}

## Pythagorean theorem

In a right triangle,
the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of squares of the other two sides:

$$a^2 + b^2 = c^2.$$

:::
This produces automatically numbered output like “Theorem 2.1 (Pythagorean theorem)” and can be referenced elsewhere in your document using @thm-pythagorean.


7.2 Example: Pythagorean theorem







Theorem 1 (Pythagorean theorem) In a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of squares of the other two sides:
\[a^2 + b^2 = c^2.\]











Example 14 (Pythagorean theorem example) For a triangle with sides 3, 4, and 5:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  3^2 + 4^2 &= 9 + 16 \\
  &= 25 \\
  &= 5^2.
\end{aligned}
\]











Definition 7 (Postulate (axiom)) A postulate (or axiom) is a statement accepted as true without proof, serving as a starting point for further reasoning.











Example 15 (Euclid’s parallel postulate) Through a point not on a line, exactly one line can be drawn parallel to the given line.
If we have line \(L\) and point \(P\) not on \(L\), only one line through \(P\) will never intersect \(L\).

title: Defining terms clearly
section: 8 Presenting a derivation: exercise, solution, theorem, proof
text:
8 Presenting a derivation: exercise, solution, theorem, proof
In teaching material, present a derivation as one or more exercises, each followed by its solution, then the theorem that records the result, with a short proof that cites the exercises. The reader meets the question before the answer, can try each step before reading it, and can find the result itself without searching through the working.
Follow these principles:

One exercise per step. Split a long derivation into exercises a reader can attempt one at a time, such as each partial derivative, then solving the resulting equations, then checking the second derivative.
The solution follows its exercise. Put each solution directly after its exercise, and give it an id named after the exercise (#exr-foo and #sol-foo), so a reader who wants to check one step can find its working.
The theorem states the result; the proof cites the exercises. The theorem gives the result in prose and as a display equation. Its proof is a few sentences that cite the exercises it rests on, not a second copy of their working.
Define notation first. Introduce any notation the exercises use in its own definition before them, not inside the theorem that follows them.
One operation per line. Inside each solution, write every displayed line with a single operation and its justification (see One operation per step).
One result per theorem. Give each theorem, corollary or lemma block a single result, with its own exercise and proof. Two results joined by a semicolon, or set side by side in one display equation, usually belong in two blocks: each can then be cited on its own, and each proof cites only the exercise it rests on.
Start from the side that simplifies. When a derivation would add and subtract a term to turn one side into the other, start from the other side instead. Simplifying an expression needs only definitions and algebra, while adding and subtracting a term asks the reader to accept a step whose purpose shows only later. Another route is to solve a definition for the term you want: add \(\mu_i\) to both sides of \(\varepsilon_i = Y_i - \mu_i\), then simplify the right-hand side to \(Y_i\), one operation per line. Adding a term to both sides of an equation is an ordinary step, not the pattern to avoid.








Definition 8 (Sample mean) The sample mean of numbers \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) is their average:
\[\bar{x} := \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i.\]











Exercise 1 (Deviations from the mean) Show that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x}) = 0,
\]
where \(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean (Definition 8).










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})
&= \sum_{i=1}^n x_i - \sum_{i=1}^n \bar{x}
&& \text{(split the sum)}\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n x_i - n \bar{x}
&& \text{(sum of a constant)}\\
&= n \bar{x} - n \bar{x}
&& \text{(}\sum_{i} x_i = n \bar{x}\text{, by the definition of } \bar{x}\text{)}\\
&= 0
&& \text{(subtract)}
\end{aligned}
\]











Theorem 2 (Deviations from the mean sum to zero) The deviations of numbers \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) from their sample mean \(\bar{x}\) (Definition 8) sum to zero:
\[\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x}) = 0.\]










ProofProof






Proof. Exercise 1 derives this result.











Example 16 (Deriving an equality from the side that simplifies) Suppose an outcome \(Y_i\) has mean \(\mu_i\) and deviation \(\varepsilon_i := Y_i - \mu_i\), and a derivation needs \(Y_i = \mu_i + \varepsilon_i\).

❌ \[
\begin{aligned}
Y_i
&= Y_i - \mu_i + \mu_i
&& \text{(add and subtract } \mu_i\text{)}\\
&= \varepsilon_i + \mu_i
&& \text{(definition of } \varepsilon_i\text{)}\\
&= \mu_i + \varepsilon_i
&& \text{(reorder the terms)}
\end{aligned}
\]
✅ \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_i + \varepsilon_i
&= \mu_i + (Y_i - \mu_i)
&& \text{(definition of } \varepsilon_i\text{)}\\
&= \mu_i + Y_i - \mu_i
&& \text{(remove the parentheses)}\\
&= Y_i + \mu_i - \mu_i
&& \text{(reorder the terms)}\\
&= Y_i + (\mu_i - \mu_i)
&& \text{(group the last two terms)}\\
&= Y_i + 0
&& \text{(} a - a = 0\text{)}\\
&= Y_i
&& \text{(} a + 0 = a\text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]

The ❌ version’s first line adds a term the reader has no reason to expect. The ✅ version starts from \(\mu_i + \varepsilon_i\), which a definition expands, and every line after that rewrites or simplifies what is already there. The ✅ version is longer because it gives a line to each step that a single “cancel” justification would hide (see One operation per step).











Example 17 (Splitting a theorem that states two results)  

❌ Theorem. Each outcome is its mean plus its deviation; given the covariates, each deviation is Gaussian with mean 0: \[Y_i = \mu_i + \varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i \mid X_i = x_i \sim \text{N}(0, \sigma^2).\]
✅ Theorem 1. Each outcome is its mean plus its deviation: \[Y_i = \mu_i + \varepsilon_i.\]
Theorem 2. Given the covariates, each deviation is Gaussian with mean 0: \[\varepsilon_i \mid X_i = x_i \sim \text{N}(0, \sigma^2).\]

The first result is algebra from the definition of \(\varepsilon_i\); the second needs the model’s distribution. In separate blocks, each gets the proof it needs, and a later step that uses only the first can cite only the first.

title: Writing for every reader
text:
NoteAI-Assisted Authorship



This chapter was written with the assistance of GitHub Copilot, which expanded on outlined ideas and draft notes provided by the author. The content represents the author’s perspective and has been reviewed for accuracy, but the detailed prose was generated through AI assistance.
Write simple, direct prose that every reader can follow. Some of your readers learned English as a second language. Some are neurodiverse. For example, some autistic readers take jokes and similes literally (W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force 2021, Use Literal Language). Some readers have a memory impairment, so a long sentence with nested clauses is hard for them to follow (W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force 2021, Avoid Double Negatives or Nested Clauses). Plain wording helps these readers most, and it helps every other reader too.
This is an equity issue. Idioms, slang, clichés, unnecessary jargon and other specialized language exclude readers who do not share the writer’s background. Those readers must first work out what the words mean, and only then can they think about the ideas. The plain language guidelines put it this way: “The first rule of plain language is: write for your audience” (Plain Language Action and Information Network 2026, Audience). Your audience includes all of these readers.
The rules in this chapter come mostly from three sources:
Each rule below comes with an example. Several rules extend sections in other chapters, and they link to those sections instead of repeating them.

title: Writing for every reader
text:
1 Use literal language
Say exactly what you mean. Do not use idioms, clichés, slang, jokes or sarcasm. An idiom is a phrase whose meaning is different from the meanings of its words, such as “blow up” for “become very large”. A reader who has not met the phrase before has to guess what it means. A reader who takes words literally may guess wrong. The W3C guidance says: “Use literal and concrete language” and “Do not use metaphors and similes unless you include an explanation” (W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force 2021, Use Literal Language). GitHub Docs says: “Avoid turns of phrase, idioms, and slang that are specific to a particular region or country” (GitHub 2026a).

❌ Which way does this course lean?
✅ Does this course put prediction or inference first?

The word “lean” in the first version is an idiom. The second version asks the literal question.
Table 1 lists more examples from statistics and machine learning.



Table 1: Idioms, clichés and slang, with literal alternatives









Idiom, cliché or slang
Literal wording




the estimates blow up
the estimates become very large


the model is a black box
we cannot read the model’s decision rule from its parameters


flexibility buys lower bias
more flexible models tend to have lower bias


this assumption costs nothing
this assumption loses no generality


a mean of zero buys one identity
a mean of zero implies one identity


Fix \(\varepsilon > 0\).
Let \(\varepsilon > 0\).


Fix a value \(t\).
Choose a value \(t\).


a ton of data
a large data set


the method falls flat on small samples
the method has high error on small samples


at the end of the day, we want low test error
our goal is low test error


Write the bias of an estimator.
Derive an expression for the bias of an estimator.


Write \(X\) in terms of \(Y\).
Express \(X\) in terms of \(Y\).


Take a sample of size \(n\) and call the sample mean \(\bar x\).
Consider a sample of size \(n\) and denote the sample mean by \(\bar x\).


the residual lies in \((-1, 1)\)
the residual is in \((-1, 1)\)


the certain distribution sits at \(0\), the uniform distribution at \(\log 4\), and the skewed distribution lies between them
the certain distribution has entropy \(0\), the uniform distribution has entropy \(\log 4\), and the skewed distribution has entropy between those two values


the two discriminant scores agree at \(x\)
the two discriminant scores are equal at \(x\)


the derivative vanishes at \(\hat\theta\)
the derivative equals \(0\) at \(\hat\theta\)


setting \(K = 2\) recovers the binary log-odds
setting \(K = 2\) gives the binary log-odds


the probability \(p\) lives in \((0, 1)\)
the probability \(p\) is in \((0, 1)\)


the linear model knows nothing about the range \([0, 1]\)
the linear model does not constrain predictions to \([0, 1]\)


Say which class the classifier predicts at \(x = 2\).
State which class the classifier predicts at \(x = 2\).






Mathematical writing has idioms too. In an exercise, “Write the bias of an estimator” means “derive an expression for the bias of an estimator”, and “Say which estimator has smaller variance” means “state which estimator has smaller variance”. A reader who takes “write” or “say” literally may copy the definition or give an informal remark instead of deriving or stating the result. Name the action instead:

“derive” for a result the reader must work out;
“express” for a rewrite in terms of other quantities;
“state” for a result the reader recalls;
“give” for a value the reader reads off.

Idioms are a kind of metaphor, so Avoid vague and metaphorical language applies to them too, and gives more examples.

title: Writing for every reader
section: 2 Use common words, and define technical ones
text:
2 Use common words, and define technical ones
Use the most common word that is still correct. The W3C guidance says to “Use common and clear words in all content” and to “Remove or explain uncommon acronyms, abbreviations, and jargon” (W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force 2021, Use Clear Words).

❌ We utilize a heuristic to ascertain the optimal number of clusters.
✅ We use the “elbow” method to choose the number of clusters: we plot the within-cluster sum of squares against the number of clusters, and pick the point where the curve stops falling steeply.

The second version uses common words, and it says what the method does instead of calling it a “heuristic”.
Some technical terms are necessary. Minimize unnecessary jargon explains when to keep a technical term and how to define it.

title: Writing for every reader
section: 3 Say when a common word has a technical meaning
text:
3 Say when a common word has a technical meaning
Many statistical terms are everyday words with a different technical meaning. Examples include bias, significant, confidence, normal, regression, error and likelihood. A reader who knows only the everyday meaning will read the sentence as a different claim. The W3C guidance says: “Do not invent new words or give words new meanings” and “Do not expect people to learn new meanings for words just to use your content” (W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force 2021, Use Clear Words). A technical course needs these terms. So say that the technical meaning differs, and give the technical meaning in plain words.

❌ The model is biased.
✅ The model is biased: at a given input, its average prediction over many training sets differs from the true mean outcome at that input. (Here bias has its statistical meaning; it does not mean the model is unfair.)

Once you define the term, use the same word for the same idea every time. The plain language guidelines say that using a different term “may cause the reader to wonder if you’re referring to the same group” (Plain Language Action and Information Network 2026, Use the same terms consistently).

❌ We split the data into a training set and a test set. We then compute the error on the held-out data.
✅ We split the data into a training set and a test set. We then compute the error on the test set.

title: Writing for every reader
text:
4 Spell out abbreviations
Write out an abbreviation the first time you use it, or replace it with a short name. The plain language guidelines say abbreviations “constantly require the reader to look back to earlier pages” (Plain Language Action and Information Network 2026, Minimize abbreviations). Do not use the Latin abbreviations e.g. and i.e.: “Few people know what they mean, and they often confuse the two” (Plain Language Action and Information Network 2026, Use examples). Write “for example” or “that is”.

❌ Tree ensembles, e.g. RF and GBM, usually reduce the MSE of a single CART.
✅ Ensembles of trees, for example random forests and boosted trees, usually have lower mean squared error than a single regression tree.

title: Writing for every reader
text:
5 Introduce shorthand before using it
Introduce every shorthand before its first use. This covers abbreviations and also shortened phrases, such as “objective” for “objective function”. Give the full term first and mark the short form, for example “an objective function, or objective for short”. Then use the short form consistently.

❌ The objective as a function of the parameters is a paraboloid. An objective function is the quantity we minimize.
✅ An objective function, or objective for short, is the quantity we minimize. The objective as a function of the parameters is a paraboloid.

title: Writing for every reader
text:
6 Write positive statements
State what is true, not what is not false. A double negative makes the reader turn “no” into “yes” before they can use the sentence. The W3C guidance says not to “use a double negative to express a positive” (W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force 2021, Avoid Double Negatives or Nested Clauses), and the plain language guidelines give the same advice (Plain Language Action and Information Network 2026, Use positive language).

❌ We do not reject the null hypothesis unless the p-value is not above 0.05.
✅ We reject the null hypothesis when the p-value is 0.05 or less.

title: Writing for every reader
section: 7 Rewrite noun strings and hidden verbs
text:
7 Rewrite noun strings and hidden verbs
A noun string is a row of nouns that act as adjectives, such as “test set error rate estimate”. The reader has to work out which noun modifies which. A hidden verb (also called a nominalization) is a verb turned into a noun, such as “perform an estimation of” in place of “estimate”. GitHub Docs advises against both. It says noun strings “can lead to incorrect translations”, and nominalizations make sentences “longer, harder to understand, and harder to translate” (GitHub 2026a). The plain language guidelines say to open up a noun string by “using more prepositions and articles” (Plain Language Action and Information Network 2026, Avoid noun strings).

❌ We report the test set error rate estimate variance.
✅ We report the variance of the estimated error rate on the test set.


❌ We performed an evaluation of the model’s prediction accuracy.
✅ We evaluated how accurately the model predicts.

title: Writing for every reader
section: 8 Put one idea in each sentence
text:
8 Put one idea in each sentence
Long sentences with nested clauses make the reader hold several unfinished ideas at once. That is hard for readers with a memory impairment (W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force 2021, Keep Text Succinct), and for readers who are translating as they go. The W3C guidance says: “Use short sentences. Have only one point per sentence” (W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force 2021, Keep Text Succinct). It also says that “Sentences that have more than one point usually have more than one linking word such as ‘and’ or ‘but’”.

❌ Because the lasso penalty, which is the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients, is not smooth at zero, some coefficients, especially when \(\lambda\) is large, are set exactly to zero.
✅ The lasso penalty is the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients. The absolute value function is not smooth at zero. Because of this, the lasso sets some coefficients exactly to zero. Usually, more coefficients are zero when \(\lambda\) is larger.

A sentence that states a result and then adds “which” and “and” clauses about it also holds several points. Give each fact its own sentence, in the order a reader needs them.

❌ The constant prediction has squared-error risk 5, which is larger than the risk 1 of the conditional mean, and strictly so because the two predictions differ.
✅ Consider the constant prediction. Its squared-error risk is 5. The risk of the conditional mean is 1. So the constant prediction has the larger risk. The inequality is strict because the two predictions differ.

Limit complex sentence structures and Lead with the subject give more examples.

title: Writing for every reader
section: 9 State every step and every point
text:
9 State every step and every point
Write every step of an argument or a procedure. Do not leave a step for the reader to fill in, and do not hint at a point you could state. The W3C guidance says readers may need “definitions or explanations for implied or ambiguous information” such as jokes, sarcasm and metaphors (W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force 2021, Explain Implied Content).

❌ Of course, nobody would use accuracy here.
✅ Do not judge this classifier by accuracy alone. Only 1% of the emails are spam, so a classifier that labels every email “not spam” has 99% accuracy but finds no spam.

The first version implies a reason and never states it. A reader who does not already know the reason learns nothing. Words like “obviously” and “clearly” hide a step in the same way; Do not substitute flippancy for support explains what to write instead.

title: Writing for every reader
section: 10 Say what numbers and symbols mean
text:
10 Say what numbers and symbols mean
Do not leave a number or a formula for the reader to interpret. Some readers find numbers hard to process (W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force 2021, Provide Alternatives for Numerical Concepts). Text-to-speech tools can also read numbers and symbols wrongly (W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force 2021, Use Clear, Unambiguous Formatting and Punctuation). The CDC Clear Communication Index scores a document on whether it explains what its numbers mean (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2026).
For a number, say what it means in words:

❌ The AUC is 0.83.
