title: Slides, posters, and figures
section: 3 Show the result in a figure
text:
3 Show the result in a figure
A figure often shows a pattern, an outlier or a comparison faster and more reliably than a sentence or a table can describe it. So when a result can be drawn, draw it, and use the text to point the reader to what the figure shows.

Show the data before summarizing them. Summary statistics can hide structure that a plot of the data reveals.
Put the key result of each section in a figure, and write the section’s text around that figure.
Make the figure show the comparison the text claims, with the groups, fitted curve or interval on the same axes.
Say in the text what to look at in the figure (see Figures and tables).
Use a table instead when readers need exact values to look up or compute with.








Example 1 (Four datasets with the same summaries) Anscombe (1973) constructed four small datasets of \((x, y)\) pairs (Wikipedia: Anscombe’s quartet). All four have the same mean of \(x\) (9), the same mean of \(y\) (7.5), the same correlation (0.82 to two decimal places) and the same least-squares line, with slope 0.5. A table of these summaries cannot tell the datasets apart. A scatterplot of each can: one is roughly linear with scatter, one follows a smooth curve, one is an exact line with a single outlier, and one has all but one of its points at the same \(x\).

title: Slides, posters, and figures
text:
4 Scientific figures
Include a figure wherever one helps a reader see a definition, an example, or a result. Draw a graph for a relationship between quantities, a diagram for a structure or a process, and a plot of the data for a fitted model or an estimate. Add figures to new work as you write it, and add them to existing chapters that lack them. On a website or slide deck, draw a graph as an interactive plotly figure where feasible, and as a 3D plotly figure where a third dimension shows the idea, such as a surface over two parameters. Keep a static image for the PDF and Word outputs, which cannot show a widget. Give every figure alt text, a numbered caption, and a code chunk that comments what the code does and why.
Lead with a well-labeled figure or table instead of a long paragraph that describes a pipeline or compares groups. Use a diagram for a conceptual model, such as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), and for a process, such as a participant flow (CONSORT) diagram or a workflow schematic. Let the text interpret what the figure shows instead of listing every number the reader can already see in it. Give the key estimates in the text and point to the figure for the rest.
A clear figure lets a reader check a result without help from the text. Before you share a figure:

Label the x-axis and y-axis clearly.
Use panel labels when a figure has several subplots.
Include enough tick marks and tick labels.
Put the ticks in the original measurement scale of each variable, however the model is parametrized and the axis is spaced. If a fit uses scaled or standardized values, place the ticks at round original values and label them with those, so a horsepower axis reads 50, 100, 150 and 200, not 0 to 1. Report numbers such as an error in the response’s units too.
Print tick labels as plain or comma-separated numbers, such as 0.001 or 10,000, not in scientific notation. A logarithmic axis is fine. Only the label format matters, so write 1, 10, 100 and 1,000, not 1e+00 through 1e+03. When the numbers are huge or tiny, rescale the units and say so in the axis title, such as “dollars (millions)”.
Use font sizes that are easy to read without dominating the plot.
Use colorblind-friendly palettes (see ColorBrewer or iwanthue).
Define colors, shapes, and line types in a legend.
Put the plot’s legend (the key to colors, shapes and line types) at the bottom of the plot, unless you have a reason to put it elsewhere. A bottom legend leaves the full plot width for the data and gives every figure the same layout.
In R, draw the static version of a figure with ggplot2, and the interactive version with plotly as described in Section 4. Present R results with modern packages gives the reasons.
Minimize abbreviations in labels and legends.
Use transparency to show overlapping data.
Show measures of precision, such as 95% confidence intervals.

For more:

Ten Simple Rules for Better Figures (Rougier et al. 2014)
Tufte CSS - style HTML articles like Edward Tufte’s books and handouts, with sidenotes, typography, and tight integration of graphics with text

title: Slides, posters, and figures
text:
5 Three-dimensional graphs
A function of two variables, such as a loss or a residual sum of squares as a function of a regression’s intercept and slope, is a surface. A contour plot shows where the function takes given values and is easy to read values from. A three-dimensional surface plot shows the same function as a landscape, so valleys, ridges and minima are visible at once. Show both when the shape of the surface matters.

Use a 3D plot for a surface, with the function’s value on the vertical axis, and pair it with a contour plot of the same function.
Do not use 3D for data that are not a surface, such as bars or pie charts: perspective makes lengths and areas harder to compare.
Choose the viewing angle so that the feature you discuss, such as the minimum, is not hidden, and label all three axes.
An interactive plot that readers can rotate, such as one made with plotly, helps on the web, but PDF and Word output show no interactive plot, so also provide a static view at a fixed angle (see Make figures accessible).
Give a 3D plot alt text that states what the surface looks like, such as “a bowl with its lowest point at …”.







NoteSource





Several of the resource links in the slide deck and figure sections began in the Benjamin-Chung Lab Manual by Jade Benjamin-Chung. The section on three-dimensional graphs is original to this guide.



For further reading, see the Professional Development and Resources chapters of the UCD-SERG lab manual.

title: Summary
text:
NoteAI-Assisted Authorship



This chapter was written with the assistance of GitHub Copilot, which expanded on outlined ideas and draft notes provided by the author. The content represents the author’s perspective and has been reviewed for accuracy, but the detailed prose was generated through AI assistance.
This chapter lists the book’s main rules as a checklist. Use the checklist when you revise a draft: read the draft once for each group of rules, and fix each passage that breaks a rule. Each rule is stated in a few words here. Follow its link for the reasons and the exceptions.

title: Summary
text:
1 Terms and notation

Define every technical term explicitly, before its first use, and follow the definition with examples and counterexamples.
Give each mathematical statement an example that applies it.
Prefer interval notation to a double inequality: \(x \in (a, b)\) rather than \(a < x < b\).
Abstract each sub-expression you are not manipulating to a symbol, such as \(\mu\) for \(\E{X}\).
Do one operation per step in a derivation, and justify each step.
Give applying a definition its own step; never skip it.
Show why you need a result before you derive it, and color each result where it is used.
Put one equals sign on each line: split a chain such as \(a = b = c\) into the rows of an aligned display.
Distinguish a function from its value.
Distinguish a random variable from its value: \(Y_i\) before the data, \(y_i\) after, and call each a “variable” or a “value” in the words too.
Use the notation that matches a quantity’s name, and keep the pairing the same everywhere.
Write each symbol through a shared macro.
Write out notational shorthands, such as the limits of a sum.
Put words between formulas, and start a sentence with a word, not a symbol.
Introduce a theorem with a complete sentence, and state it so that it stands alone.
Spell out a number used as an adjective, and write the numeral for a number used as a name.

title: Summary
text:
2 Claims and evidence

Support every claim with a citation or with data.
Do not substitute flippancy for support, such as calling a step “trivial”.
Cite a relevant source that is trustworthy.
Copy exact wording with caution, even from your own earlier work.
Cite a source once per passage.
Link liberally to the sources and tools that you mention.
Quote the original rather than a source that quotes it.
Put the content first: name the topic, not its author, in headings and sentences.

title: Summary
text:
3 Papers

Write to clarify your thinking: write each question or idea down as it comes.
Follow the standard structure of a research paper.
Organize the Results section to fit the design of the study.
Label variables in plain words in figures and tables.
Use descriptive subsection headings.
Avoid forward references: move the content ahead of the sentence that uses it.
Put each link to a video next to the text that it supports.
Follow the journal’s conventions for a manuscript, and check the submission checklist before you submit.

title: Summary
text:
4 Words

Prefer plain words to Latin-derived ones where a plain word says the same thing.
Avoid vague and metaphorical language.
Follow an abstract statement with an example.
Replace the word “thing” with the object, quantity, step, or idea that it stands for.
Give a technical word one meaning.
Minimize unnecessary jargon.
Edit out clusters of clichéd words and sentence shapes, which make prose read as generic or machine-drafted.
Say what something is before what it is not.

title: Summary
text:
5 Writing for every reader

Use literal language.
Use common words, and define technical ones.
Say when a common word has a technical meaning, such as “significant” or “bias”.
Spell out abbreviations.
Write positive statements, and avoid double negatives.
Rewrite noun strings and hidden verbs.
Put one idea in each sentence.
State every step and every point.
Say what numbers and symbols mean.
Use examples that every reader knows.
Keep a predictable structure.
Present ideas in more than one form.
Test your writing with a reader.

title: Summary
text:
6 Sentences

Keep relative pronouns such as “that” and “which”.
Follow “this” or “that” with the noun that it refers to.
Follow a quantifier such as “both” or “each” with its noun.
Avoid garden-path sentences.
Name the object of a relational noun.
Lead with the subject.
Make every word tell: cut words that carry no meaning, but keep detail that does.
Limit complex sentence structures.
Do not rule out readings that no reader would make.
Write about the subject, not about the text.
Put a list of three or more phrases in bullet points.

title: Summary
text:
7 Teaching materials

Build the lecture from exercises and solutions.
Ask the question before giving the definition.
Present a derivation as an exercise and solution, then the theorem and its proof.
Give each defined term its own div.
State the notation and its alternatives.
Lead with the simplest correct form of a definition.
Reuse one written version of each result.
Use real data and compute every number.
Show each idea applied and in a figure.
Write labs in both R and Python that run on any computer.
Make figures accessible.
Structure slides for the reader.
Credit another course’s material in a collapsed “Source” callout, not in running prose.
Do not formally acknowledge material borrowed from your own work, and remove any existing credit to your own work, but keep what that work itself credits.

title: Summary
text:
8 Software text

Say what changed and why in a pull request or commit message.
Comment why, not what.
Write release notes by their effect on the user.

title: Summary
text:
9 Thinking

Write the question down first.
Send a written question that gives the reader the context to answer it.
Draft the plan before you run the analysis.

title: Word choice
text:
NoteAI-Assisted Authorship



This chapter was written with the assistance of GitHub Copilot, which expanded on outlined ideas and draft notes provided by the author. The content represents the author’s perspective and has been reviewed for accuracy, but the detailed prose was generated through AI assistance.
I recommend trying to replace Latin-derived words and phrases with Old English-derived equivalents (“Anglish” words) where possible; it generally makes writing simpler and easier to read. Latin words  create artificial barriers to understanding. Many Latin-derived words commonly used in scientific writing are composed from roots and affixes which are not commonly used in their basic forms; hence, readers cannot determine the meanings of these words by decomposing them. Instead, they need to memorize the meanings of these words directly. In contrast, the components of composite Anglish words are typically also used individually, so the meanings of the composites can be derived directly. Table 1 lists some common Latinate words and phrases and Anglish alternatives.
See also https://bark-fa.github.io/Anglish-Translator/
Overused vocabulary lists more words, many of them Latin-derived, that writers reach for by reflex, with plainer alternatives.
I am aware that this book, and even this chapter, contains many Latin word choices where there are Anglish alternatives. It is a work in progress, and also, I am not advocating 100% Anglish purity. Use whichever words and phrases you think your readers are most likely to understand easily. Preferring Anglish is merely a useful heuristic to help achieve our ultimate goal of producing clear, easy-to-read writing.
Just to be clear, although I prefer Anglish words, I have no particular preference for Anglish people or culture; it is only a practical consideration, based on the realities of English as the current default language of science and the relatively-recent hybridization of the English language.

title: Word choice
text:
1 Avoid vague and metaphorical language
Scientific claims should be precise enough to test. Vague or metaphorical phrases can sound evocative, but they leave the reader guessing at the specific quantity or mechanism you mean. Whenever you can, replace a metaphor with the precise term for the thing you are describing. Table 2 lists some common vague phrases and more precise alternatives.



Table 2: Vague or metaphorical phrases and more precise alternatives





Vague or metaphorical
More precise




infection pressure
incidence rate


disease burden
incidence rate, or prevalence proportion


the signal was strong
the effect size was large


a huge effect
a risk ratio of 4.2






The precise alternative is not always shorter, but it tells the reader exactly which quantity you measured, which makes your claim verifiable. When a metaphor genuinely aids intuition, state the precise quantity first, then offer the metaphor as a secondary aid.
Informal idioms are metaphors too. “Kicks in”, “the whole point” and “getting there” stand in for a literal claim; state the claim. Use literal language explains why idioms exclude some readers, and gives more examples. Stock metaphors such as “pave the way” and “shed light on” are clichés, and Overused vocabulary lists more of them.
Money words are idioms too when no money is involved. “Costs us”, “buys us” and “at the price of” borrow from commerce to describe a trade-off, and the reader must translate them back. Say what is lost or gained. Keep a literal use: a computational cost, a monetary cost, or a cost function that the text defines as a term.

❌ Nesting the cross-validation loop costs another factor of \(K\) in computing time.
✅ Nesting the cross-validation loop multiplies the computing time by \(K\).


❌ Continuity buys us the intermediate value theorem.
✅ Continuity gives us the intermediate value theorem.


❌ The penalty costs us a little flexibility at the ends of the curve.
✅ The penalty reduces the curve’s flexibility a little at its ends.

Some single words cause a different problem. Words such as “obviously”, “clearly” and “trivially” can assert that a claim needs no support instead of supplying any. Do not substitute flippancy for support says when those words are a problem and what to write instead.

title: Word choice
section: 2 Follow an abstract statement with an example
text:
2 Follow an abstract statement with an example
An abstract or general statement is fine, as long as a concrete example follows it. A vague statement is not: one that names no specific case leaves the reader to invent one, and they may invent the wrong one.
For example, consider this bullet from a list of what machine learning needs:

statistics to say what a finite sample of data supports

The bullet is general, which is fine. What it lacks is an instance that shows the reader what “supports” means. Adding one turns it into something a reader can check:

statistics to say what a finite sample of data supports: if most of the spam in a pile of training emails mentions money, statistics tells us whether that pattern should hold for next month’s emails or is a quirk of this particular pile

When you write a general claim, ask what one specific case of it looks like, and put that case right after the claim.

title: Word choice
text:
3 Say which thing
The word thing almost never survives a second look. Name the object, quantity, step or idea it stands for.

❌ The main thing to check is the residuals.
✅ Check the residuals first.

The plural and the filler phrases built on it (“a number of things”, “other things”, “things like that”) are the same problem. Each one tells the reader that something exists without saying what.

❌ Several things can inflate the standard errors.
✅ Correlated predictors and clustered observations can inflate the standard errors.

If you cannot name the object, quantity, step or idea, the sentence is not yet ready to write.

title: Word choice
section: 4 Give a technical word one meaning
text:
4 Give a technical word one meaning
A word that names a technical concept keeps that one meaning on every page. Two fields often use the same word for different concepts. When a reader meets the word in its second sense, they must stop and work out which concept the sentence means.
Pick the word’s established meaning in the course sequence, and name the other concept with a different phrase. If the other field’s word is still useful, list it as a labeled alias in the definition of the concept it names.
For example, hypothesis means a statistical hypothesis: a claim about a population, such as a null hypothesis that a test examines. In machine learning, hypothesis also names a candidate prediction function.

❌ The learner picks one hypothesis from the hypothesis set.
✅ The learner picks one function from the prediction function family.

The definition of the prediction function family can then say that machine-learning texts call it a hypothesis class or hypothesis space.

title: Word choice
text:
5 Write the full phrase
Do not leave out words the phrase needs to be complete. A clipped phrase such as “the true mean function” asks the reader to supply the missing words, and the reader may supply different ones than you meant. Readers who are learning English, and readers who read literally, cannot always recover them. Name what the object is a function of, and what it is conditional on.
The same rule applies to symbols. Write a function with its argument, such as \(\truemeanf{\predvar}\), not the bare function name, unless the sentence is about the function as a whole and the page has said so. A symbol in a sentence should look like the same symbol in the display equation it refers to.







Example 1 (Writing the full phrase and the argument) The display equation is \(\Outvar = \truemeanf{\predvar} + \noise\).

❌ The outcome variable is the true mean function plus noise.
✅ The outcome variable is the true mean function of the outcome variable given the input value \(\predvar\), namely \(\truemeanf{\predvar}\), plus noise.

title: Word choice
text:
6 Choose each preposition on purpose
A preposition states a relationship between two things. Small words such as of, for, with and using are easy to reach for by reflex, and each one can stand for many different relationships (ownership, purpose, cause, part and whole, tool, source). When the sentence does not say which relationship it means, the reader has to guess. Readers who are learning English, and readers who read literally, guess worst.
For each preposition, ask what relationship it states. If you cannot answer in one phrase, replace it with a verb that names the relationship.







Example 2 (Naming the relationship)  

❌ The error of the prediction is large.
✅ The prediction misses the observed outcome by a large amount.

Of could mean the error the prediction makes, the error in the way it was computed, or an error that belongs to the prediction in some other way. The verb misses says which.

❌ We fit the model for the training set.
✅ We estimate the model’s coefficients from the training set.

For could mean on behalf of, in order to serve, or using. From states the relationship exactly: the training set is the source of the estimates.




Keep a plain preposition when it states the relationship exactly, such as in for location and by for the agent of a passive verb.

title: Word choice
text:
7 Minimize unnecessary jargon
Jargon is vocabulary specific to a field. Some jargon is necessary: a precise technical term can replace a long explanation, and readers in the field expect it. But jargon becomes a barrier when a normal word would work just as well, or when you use a common word with a special, field-specific meaning without defining it.
Prefer normal words used in their usual sense. When you do need a technical term, define it clearly at first use, then keep using the same term rather than switching between synonyms. When the field itself uses several names for the concept, list them where you define it (see Name the synonyms).







Example 3 (Replacing unnecessary jargon)  

❌ We leveraged a bespoke pipeline to operationalize the ingestion of heterogeneous data modalities.
✅ We wrote a custom program to combine data from several sources.

The plain version is shorter, and it states what was actually done.




For each technical word, ask whether it carries meaning that a plainer word would lose. If it does not, replace it with the plainer word. If it does carry necessary meaning but a reader outside your subfield would not understand it, define it clearly at first use.

title: Principles of Scientific Writing
text:
This website presents my perspective on writing in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM), with a focus on writing about statistical data analysis. Most of its rules also apply to informative prose in general. I intend to give it to academic mentees as a style guide reference, and also use it as a notebook for myself.
The Introduction describes the book’s scope and readers, and how to use its chapters. The Summary lists the book’s main rules as a checklist for revising a draft.


The site’s structure ultimately derives from the Benjamin-Chung Lab Manual. For further reading, see the UCD-SERG lab manual and the qwt website template.
